div.p: Nature relatedness is an individual difference characteristic defined as an interconnected feeling between the self and nature (Nisbet et al., 2009). Previous meta-analytic research suggests that nature related individuals are happier (Capaldi et al., 2014;Pritchard et al., 2020). The literature suggests nature related individuals may be happier because they are more likely to go out into nature, which promotes well-being. However, it could also be partly because nature-related individuals may be noticing more nature around them at any given moment, which has not been previously tested. In this dissertation, I examined the possibility that highly nature related individuals notice more nature in urban scene images. Items of the Nature Relatedness scale (Nisbet et al., 2009) propose noticing nature behaviours that fit in the self-concept of a person high on the trait. Still, no research has explored behavioural measures of momentary noticing nature in this association. In this dissertation, noticing was explored through two distinct processes, perception and attention, with the research split into two phases. Perception (Phase 1) is characterized as what an individual interprets as nature in an urban scene. Attention (Phase 2) is operationalized in two ways: the first objects seen in an image (first attention) and voluntary attention paid to pleasant objects in the images. I hypothesized that nature related individuals would perceive more nature, notice nature first, and focus more on the nature in the images than individuals lower on nature relatedness. Contrary to the hypothesis, there was no association between perception of nature and nature relatedness in Phase 1. However, there was an association between attention being paid towards nature and nature relatedness in Phase 2, where nature related individuals had their attention drawn to nature first and chose to focus their attention on it. There is also some preliminary support that nature related people's ability to notice nature may be a reason they are happier in general. This study is the first to utilize iii behavioural tasks to explore if nature related individuals do, in fact, notice more nature in urban environments.

One of the largest impacts of the industrial revolution was the transformation of our manufacturing processes and workplaces. This shift led to a surge in people relocating to larger cultural and economic centers. Thus, most people were no longer living in rural environments, but rather in urban areas. For example, in the 1920s, only 50% of Canadians lived in cities; in 2015, this number increased to 80% (Stelter & Artibise, 2015). Within the next 20 years, around the world, it is projected that 70% of people will be living in urban cities (Ritchie & Roser, 2018). As more people move to cities, the more cities must expand and reduce the natural areas to make room for more development (McKinney, 2008). This shift has changed our access to nature, which may be impeding our interactions with it. This reduction of experiences can be detrimental to our well-being because spending time in nature has previously been associated with physical, emotional, social, and spiritual well-being (Chowdhury, 2019). If we spend less time in nature, we may lose out on its benefits.

Even with much research showing the benefits of spending time in nature on our wellbeing, the definition and metric of nature in research have not been consistent across the literature. The Merriam-Webster Dictionary (n.d.) defines nature as a physical environment free from human production. This physical environment of nature can encompass many things, such as forests, bodies of water, plants, wildlife, and rocks, to name a few. In research, there are many different ways authors define nature in their articles, with nature being characterized as environments such as forests, urban parks, blue spaces (e.g. beaches, marinas, lakes), or even just trees in a neighbourhood. When Taylor and Hochuli (2017) explored the definition of greenspace in 125 articles across multiple disciplines, it was clear there was no single unified definition of greenspace; across the literature, the authors found that there was a range of operational definitions, interpretations, and even a lack of clear articulation about what the author meant by using the term greenspace. Minimal forms of nature, such as indoor foliage or views of nature outside their windows, also count as nature in the literature. Additionally, some research utilizes nature activities or indirect nature exposure, such as images, videos, art, or biophilic architecture as forms of nature. Altogether this suggests that many different forms of nature may count, but more minimal and indirect forms of nature may still differ from larger, more expansive forms of nature, such as the forest.

Outside of research, individual people can also differ in their definition of nature. For example, when Vining et al. (2008) asked participants how they defined nature, approximately 47% of people reported that nature was defined as untouched by humans or not human-made.

However, even if they felt that nature had to be untouched by humans, over 75% of people reported feeling part of nature (when asked if they felt a part or separate from nature; Vining et al., 2008). Therefore, even with less chance to interact with nature, people still seem to connect and feel a part of it. This feeling of being a part of nature is characterized as nature connectedness (nature relatedness). Nature connectedness is a trait defined by an individual's feeling as being one with nature, caring for nature, and wanting to protect it (Schutlz, 2002).

Previous research suggests that individuals who identify as connecting more to nature than others tend to be happier in general. Two meta-analyses have shown that nature connection is positively related to well-being indicators, such as pleasant emotional balance, life satisfaction, and purpose in life (Capaldi et al., 2014;Pritchard et al., 2020). There are a few suggestions for why we see this relationship. It could be that nature connected individualsfoot_0 are interacting with nature more than those who are not as nature connected. One way they could be doing this is by being more likely to be out in nature, which has previously been associated with well-being (see review Capaldi et al., 2015). The other way is that nature connected people may be noticing more nature in their everyday urban lives, with or without differences in objective nature contact. The current dissertation examines the possibility of the latter. Specifically, the main goal of the dissertation is to examine if nature connected individuals are more likely to "notice" nature in an urban environment. Three studies, split into two separate phases, were run. The three studies used behavioural measures of noticing nature rather than relying on broad self-report items generally used to measure nature connection. For example, the item highlighted in the title ("Even in the middle of the city, I notice nature around me"; Nisbet et al., 2009) used to score an individual's nature connection (nature relatedness) may be more a belief of the self than actualized behaviours in real-life situations. I used urban images with a controlled amount of nature to explore if nature connected individuals noticed the nature in the urban environments.

div.head: Nature and Well-being
div.p: One of environmental psychology's many focuses is nature research, and even more specifically, addressing how nature is beneficial for humans. Much research suggests that spending time with nature or connecting with nature is beneficial in many ways. There are physical benefits of nature exposure that can be both mental and bodily. For instance, research has shown that exposing ourselves to nature, such as walking in nature (Basu et al., 2019;Berman et al., 2008), seeing nature images (Gamble et al., 2014), and even nature sounds (Van Hedger et al., 2019) help with attention control, usually tested through attention tasks in labs (Stenfors et al., 2019). This is the case for both children and adults. Nature exposure is also helpful for child development. For example, children who had access to more greenness had more imaginative play than those in an ordinary school (through green schools; Dowdell et al., 2011), were more self-disciplined (Taylor et al., 2002), developed more motor skills (White, 2004), had better academic performance (Sivarajah et al., 2018), and developed more problemsolving skills (Leiberman et al. 1998). Research also suggests that the amount of time spent in greenspaces in childhood was related to lower levels of psychiatric disorders in adulthood (Engemann et al., 2019). Nature is also used as a therapeutic tool for mental illness (see review:

div.head: Harper et al., 2021).
div.p: There are also physiological and self-report markers of health shown to be better with more nature exposure. For example, Ulrich and colleagues (1991;1983) found that nature views, images, or videos were good for surgical recovery, pain tolerance, and stress reduction.

Additionally, White and colleagues (2019) showed that those who reported spending more time in nature (defined as "open spaces in and around towns and cities, including parks, canals, and nature areas; the coast and beaches; and the countryside, including farmland, woodland, hills, and rivers" p. 8) reported better general physical health and felt more satisfied with their life than those who did not spend any time in nature. The researchers found a significant increase between 0 and 120 minutes spent a week in nature, but there were diminishing returns after 120 minutes (i.e. levelling off). A study conducted in Toronto examined the health benefits of neighbourhood trees. Researchers examined the objective number of trees in a neighbourhood through mapping data and subjective ratings of overall health and diagnosis for numerous medical and mental health conditions. The researchers found that those living in a neighbourhood with more trees self-reported better overall health and fewer cardio-metabolic disorders (Kardan et al., 2015b).
There was no significant relationship between the number of trees in a neighbourhood and other disorders, such as mental disorders and other illnesses (cancer, migraines, asthma, or arthritis).

The authors reported that having ten trees in your block would predict an increase of .04 units in a 1 to 5 scale of health perception, which was equivalent to an increase of your annual household income by $10,200 or being seven years younger. Hunter et al. (2019) examined the amount of time spent in a natural environment to see a physiological reduction in stress through cortisol and alpha-amylase hormones. They saw that after participants spent 21 to 30 minutes in nature, there was a reduction in both stress hormones, but there were diminishing returns after 30 minutes of exposure.

div.head: Nature and Happiness
div.p: Nature is also related to emotional and psychological well-being. One way this can be characterized is a person's feeling of happiness. Diener (1984) proposed that for a person to feel happy, they would emotionally feel good in day-to-day life and have positive cognitive judgements about their life overall. This view encapsulates the term subjective well-being.

Positive affect, negative affect, and satisfaction with life generally fall under this term. Affect is defined by experienced feelings, such as moods (Diener et al., 2010). In research, this is usually tested by asking participants to report how often they felt (i.e. recall) or how much they are currently feeling various emotions (i.e. state). A person's trait level affect is an aggregate of state feelings over time. Life satisfaction is an individual's judgment that their life events have gone well and they are happy (satisfied) with their life (Diener et al., 1985). The overall assessment of life satisfaction arrives from each person's idiosyncratic criteria of what it means to be satisfied with life.
However, others suggest that subjective well-being may be too narrow of a characterization of happiness and may be missing out on other factors that describe a good life.

For example, Ryff (1989) argues that happiness or positive well-being comes from more extensive psychological markers and proposes the Six-Factor model of Psychological Wellbeing. Ryff's (1989) model is characterized by six factors: meaning in life, personal growth, autonomy, personal mastery, positive relationship with others, and self-acceptance. To date, there are many other markers or ways to assess how a person is flourishing in their life that scholars describe as eudaimonic indicators (see review by VanderWeele, 2017). The term eudaimonic well-being is widely debated on its definition and the markers of well-being that fit within it (Huta & Waterman, 2014). Still, these markers are commonly explored to examine well-being and its association with nature (see Calpaldi et al., 2015 for a review on the ways nature is associated with a person flourishing in life).
Nature contact relates to a range of psychological and emotional well-being indicators.

For one, meta-analytic work on the effect of nature exposure on affect (both positive and negative) across 32 studies in 6 different countries (Japan, USA, Canada, Sweden, Netherlands, and the UK) suggests that being exposed to nature increases positive affect and decreases negative affect; however, the relationship between negative affect and nature is not as strong (but still significant; McMahan & Estes, 2015). They also found no difference between the natureaffect relationship in two types of nature: wild nature (e.g. forest) and managed nature (e.g. urban walking trail). Additionally, both actual nature exposure and lab-simulated nature exposure were found to be beneficial for mood, but actual nature exposure (15 studies) was better than lab-simulated exposure (16 studies;McMahan & Estes, 2015).

Further, White and colleagues (2019) showed that the odds of someone reporting good well-being (measured through a single life satisfaction item) was higher for those spending more time in nature (at least 60 minutes per week) than those not spending any time in nature. This relationship saw a linear increase (of the odds ratio) from 0 minutes to 120 minutes a week and diminishing returns after that. Though, other research suggests that even spending at least 5 minutes outside was shown to increase both positive affect and feelings of awe (Neill et al., 2019).

Even everyday nature experiences have been related to mood. For example, those who travelled more in green and blue spaces experienced a generally higher positive mood (Glasgow et al., 2019). Further, if they travelled through more dense, compact environments, such as more urban-type areas, they were more likely to see a decrease in their moods. Also, those momentarily outdoors or even doing outdoor activities, such as gardening, bird/nature watching, walking, or hiking, reported being happier on a single-item happiness measure (MacKerron & Mourato, 2013). This was examined through GPS data of locations (i.e. more objective indicator of nature). In another study, when people reported being in nature, they reported more state vitality (defined as feeling alive, alert, and energized), over and above social interactions, presence of weekends, and even if the activity they were doing was physical activity (Ryan et al., 2010). This was also seen during the COVID-19 pandemic, where those spending time outdoors felt happier (single item; Stieger et al., 2021), and in particular, those doing activities that may be viewed as an activity engaged with nature, such as walking, gardening and bird watching showed higher levels of positive affect (Lades et al., 2020). Altogether, this suggests that nature contact is related to happiness.

div.head: Why do we see benefits from being exposed to nature?
div.p: The biophilia hypothesis describes a tendency for humans to have an innate urge to connect with other forms of living things, such as nature and wildlife (Wilson, 1984). Biophilia comes from the Greek term meaning love of life or living things. The hypothesis stems from our understanding of our evolutionary history in nature. Humans have spent the large majority of our existence dependent on nature for our survival. We need to understand our local surroundings to read the weather, the movement of our prey, the local plant life that can be used and consumed, and how to protect ourselves from our predators. Therefore, we have evolved to process information about the local place, its plants, wildlife, and surroundings and be drawn to the healthy parts.

More than just being drawn to healthy nature, there are theories about why we may see the benefits from spending time in nature. One of these theories is the Attention Restoration Theory (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989). As we have moved away from nature and into a more urban environment, we have to try to process new information about highways, automobiles, shopping centres, workplaces, to name a few, that we have not evolved to process. Therefore, with its bright lights, loud sounds, and stressful everyday life demands, the urban environment overstimulates and makes us feel fatigued. Kaplan and Kaplan (1989) describe these stimulations of urban living as hard fascinations. They suggest that nature can be a soft fascination that allows one to feel restored, which characterizes the theory. Four characteristics define a soft fascination:

the soft fascination must: 1) allow for a sense of being away from the hard fascination; 2) allow you to keep your attention or fascination with minimal effort; 3) be large enough to explore and; 4) it must also elicit feelings of pleasure. Nature fits these four characteristics. The Attention Restoration theory claims that to feel restored, we need to find soft fascination to reduce the effects of the hard fascinations in our lives. However, the nature effect on cognitive performance has been mixed in the literature (as identified by Stenfors et al., 2019). When Stenfors and colleagues (2019) explored this effect in a pooled dataset of 13 experiments performed in the Berman lab, they found that nature exposure improved attention post-experience compared to urban environments. This effect was even stronger after controlling for the ordering effect of conditions. Therefore, spending time in nature can be beneficial for attention and restoration.

Additionally, our modern world is full of stressors that trouble us. Previously, our ancestors would get physiological responses from dangers around them that would trigger their fight or flight instinct. Once the threat was gone, their bodily response would go back to normal (going through the "stress cycle" as coined by Nagoski & Nagoski, 2020). Stressors in our daily lives can also trigger these physiological responses, but do not necessarily go away in the short term. Therefore, it is hard to indicate to the body that you are safe to move out of the stress response. The Stress Reduction Theory proposes that exposing ourselves to nature helps reduce the psychological (i.e. negative affect) and physiological response (e.g. stress hormones; Ulrich et al., 1991) to stress. The theory proposes that healthy nature (that we are drawn to) tells our bodies that everything is okay and safe to relax. Therefore, we see a physiological reduction in stress hormones by spending time in nature (Yao et al., 2021;Hunter et al., 2019) and thus, go through our stress cycle.
The previously described research on the relationship between nature and well-being is, in general, consistent with all of the theories on why we may see the benefit of nature

. Both the Attentional Restoration Theory and the Stress Reduction Theory highlight the evolutionary connection with nature (i.e. the biophilic effect). From these theories, there are three more recent theoretical approaches to the benefits from nature, as highlighted in a book chapter by Joye and van den Berg (2018). The first is perceptual fluency. For both the Attentional Restoration Theory and the Stress Reduction Theory, natural environments can be easier to process cognitively than the visual information coming from urban environments making them more familiar and less fatiguing to see due to our evolutionary connection to nature. The second approach is nature connection. The authors suggest that "people gain purpose and meaning in life by feeling that they belong in the natural world" (p. 62; also see Passmore & Howell, 2014 review). Again, implying for both the Attentional Restoration Theory and the Stress Reduction Theory, feeling a
part of the natural world would make people feel more comfortable and safe in the environment.

In addition, research supports the proposition that nature connection (relatedness) is a psychological need (Baxter & Pelletier, 2019). The last approach is micro-experiences with nature. They suggest that over time, people accumulate a large number of micro-experiences with nature, such as viewing natural scenes out of a window, in art, television, or even reading books about nature, that improve a person's well-being and creates a way to mitigate negative feelings from everyday stressors (also see review Passmore & Howell., 2014). Altogether, these theories propose that our connection, dependence, and preference for healthy and safe nature are vital for our well-being (both physical and psychological) because of our evolutionary interconnection with nature. The differences across the theories come from the details of the processes or mechanisms of our interactions of nature (e.g. reduction in stress, feelings of restoration, etc.). However, no matter the theory (or its processes and mechanisms), the benefit of nature are quite robust.

div.head: Extinction of Experience
div.p: In our urban world, people spend more time indoors than out in nature. For example,

Canadians spend approximately 90% of their time inside and report only spending 6% of their time outdoors (Matz et al., 2015), which does not necessarily indicate they are spending any of that time in natural environments. Additionally, in the Canadians at Work and Home Statistics Canada Social survey, 26% of participants reported they did not participate in any type of outdoor activity (e.g. fishing/hunting, camping, hiking, wildlife viewing) over the past 12 months (Statistics Canada, 2018). When examining the changes in our experiences with nature, research shows that children spend less time in nature over the generations (using both census data and interviews; Gaster, 1991). The generational shift characterizes the Extinction of Experience (Pyles, 1993); it is the generational loss of interaction between humans and nature (Gaston & Soga, 2020;Soga & Gaston, 2016). Even with the term extinction, it does not mean that we have entirely lost our experience with nature. Instead, it is more a discussion about our reduction in our contact and interaction with nature. Research showed that contact with nature in childhood predicted continued contact with nature in adulthood (D'amore, 2016;Pensini et al., 2016;Rosa et al., 2018). If people are being exposed less to nature as children, they are likely to not spend as much time in nature as adults and then not expose their children to nature. This perpetuates a cycle in reducing our contact with nature. Therefore, the more we are missing our experiences with nature, the baseline average of time spent in nature for each generation diminishes.

However, some research suggests that there is no difference in the amount of time kids are spending in nature (when comparing two surveys a contemporary one and one from early 1900), but rather it is the differences in the activities they are doing in nature (Novotny et al., 2021).

The reduction of connection with nature can also be seen in indirect ways (compared to only direct contact with nature). We are witnessing the loss of nature connection and importance in cultural products. For instance, research on literature, film, and television has shown a decrease in nature depictions. Between 1937 and 2010, there has been a decrease in nature (even more so wild, untamed nature) in Disney and Pixar animated feature movies over the years, in addition to a reduction in the biodiversity of the non-anthropomorphized animals present in the films (Prévot-Julliard et al., 2014). Also, after the 1950s, there was a decline in nature words in English fiction novels, song lyrics, and movie storylines internationally (Kesebir & Kesebir, 2017). In 2007, the Oxford Junior Dictionary removed approximately 50 nature terms. Terms such as beaver and dandelion were replaced by words such as Blog and MP3 player (Dhillon, 2008). When Voneeta Gupta, the head of the Oxford Junior Dictionary, was interviewed about the removal of words, she gave other examples of nature words that have previously been As the generations are losing their experiences in nature, they are also missing out on the many benefits of spending time in nature, such as the health and psychological benefits. Thus, there is clear value to creating awareness about the extinction of experience problem and promoting nature connection. Shanahan and colleagues (2015a) suggest the importance of two interventions to help with the extinction of experience. First, the authors suggest introducing more urban nature to expose to people. Research on five metropolitan cities around the world (Tucson, Arizona, USA; Berlin, Germany; Washington DC, USA; Florence, Italy; and Chiba, Japan) indicates that even if the cities may have a large portion of biodiversity (measured through plants and birds), the majority of the residents live in areas that have a below-average amount of biodiversity (Turner et al., 2004). This is problematic as objective amount of nature, such as neighbourhood tree canopy, has previously been associated with well-being, such as general health (Kardan et al., 2015b). This suggests that adding more nature to neighbourhoods may benefit residents. To make a city greener, adding greenspaces and trees in neighbourhoods, making nature more accessible, and utilizing biophilic design (characterized as bringing nature exposure through incorporating natural elements in built environments by mimicking or specifically using them; Kellert & Calabrese, 2015) could be implemented. The second intervention suggested by the authors was to find ways to connect people to the nature they already have around them. Richardson and colleagues (2021) propose the importance of showing people how to connect to nature rather than solely giving them the opportunity to be in contact with it. In this study, they had UK participants report their time spent in natural environments (such as visiting local parks, greenspaces, rivers, or forested areas) and also how often they did noticing nature activities (such as looking at natural scenery, taking pictures or videos of nature, listening to bird songs, smelling flowers, or studying natural areas, to name a few). Those who participated in more noticing nature activities were more likely to feel connected to nature than those who just spent a lot of time in nature. Said another way, having people take notice of nature can be more helpful in connecting people with nature (i.e. reducing the effects of the extinction of experience) than solely giving better access for nature contact. Still, it is also important to understand who may already be spending time in the nature available to them and who may be embracing the "magic of mundane" (Dobson et al., 2021) in urban nature (i.e. who is noticing the nature already around them?).

div.head: Nature Connectedness
div.p: Even with an evolutionary urge to connect to nature, we still see individual differences in the extent one feels connected with nature. Nature connectedness is characterized as the psychological interaction between an individual and nature, making the individual feel a part or at one with nature (Lengieza & Swim, 2021). Nature connection has been examined as both traitlike and state. State nature connection refers to the experience when an individual feels a sense of connection with nature in the moment, usually stemming from their current exposure to natural surroundings. In contrast, trait-like nature connection is a stable feeling and understanding of connection to nature. For this dissertation, I focus on the trait-like nature connection. Previously, many different measures and scales have been created to assess the trait, such as Emotional Affinity Towards Nature (EATN; Kals et al., 1999), Connectedness to Nature (CNT; Mayer & Frantz, 2004), Commitment to Nature (COM; Davis et al., 2009), Environmental Identity (EID; Clayton, 2003), Connectivity with nature (CWN; Dutcher et al., 2007), Inclusion of Nature in Self (INS; Schultz, 2002), the Extended Inclusion of Nature in Self (EINS; Martin & Czellar, 2016), and Nature Relatedness (NR; Nisbet et al., 2009). Previously, Tam (2013) highlighted the similarities across the different nature connection measures (all but the EINS). First, they are all highly correlated (r values all above .40). Second, in factor analyses, they all have an underlying higher-order construct of connection to nature. This indicates they are examining the similar factor of nature connection. Third, the pattern of relationships with discriminant validity measures, such as personality, well-being, and environmentalism, was similar, but of modestly varying degrees. Altogether, this suggests that none of the different measures of nature connection are clearly best to use for this dissertation. I have, however, chosen to explore the relationships with the Nature Relatedness scale.

Nature relatedness is defined as feelings of interconnection between the self and other living beings (Nisbet et al., 2009). Nisbet and colleagues (2009) created the construct to incorporate physical, cognitive, and affective connections with nature. For example, it contains pro-environmental feelings/views, love for nature, seeing the importance of unappealing nature, and self-identity as an environmental/nature person. The measure includes three distinct facets (derived from exploratory factor analyses): 1) the Self, 2) Experience, and 3) Perspective. The self scale encompasses identification of the interconnection with nature, such as affective feelings towards nature and reflective thought about how actions may affect nature. The experience facet consists of physical contact with nature, such as the degree of comfort and desire to be in nature. The perspective facet embodies worldviews towards nature, such as humans' impacts on the planet.

Some research has explored how trait-like nature relatedness can predict different behaviours and attitudes. For example, nature relatedness has predicted love for animals (Nisbet et al., 2009), environmentalism (Mackay & Schmitt, 2019), physical activity, and less screentime (Molina-Cando et al., 2021). Previous research also suggests the relationship between nature connection (more general and also specifically with nature relatedness) and subjective well-being. The trait level of nature connection was related to both hedonic well-being (positive affect and life satisfaction) and eudaimonic well-being (Ryff's psychological well-being [1989] and vitality; Capaldi et al., 2014;Pritchard et al., 2020) in meta-analyses. More specifically, nature relatedness had a small mean effect size for happiness (r = .18; aggregating well-being markers; Capaldi et al., 2014), hedonic well-being (r = .19) and eudaimonic well-being (r = .22; Pritchard et al., 2020) across multiple studies examining these relationships. Therefore, not only are those who spend time in nature happy, but those who feel more connected to nature report that they are happier people overall.

It could be that even though the general population is interacting less with nature (extinction of experience), people who identify as nature connected may be finding ways to interact with nature, which makes them happier people. This would fit with general understandings of the self and the self-concept. The self is the conscious part of you that thinks, decides and acts in a certain way (Myers et al., 2015). The self is made up of the self-esteem (sense of worth), the social self (role with other people), the self-knowledge (how a person describes themselves), and the self-concept (description of whom a person thinks they are). A person who feels or identifies as nature connected would find ways to interact or connect with nature to fit their self-concept. For example, in terms of spending time in nature or connecting with it, it is the self that decides to go out and notice nature. Nature can also help form our identity and self-concept (Passmore & Howell, 2014). For example, nature can do this by allowing us to compare ourselves to other animals (Myers, 2003), find attachment with our local environments (Taylor, 2007), to reflect about ourselves (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989), and even help heighten our self-awareness (Mayer et al., 2009). Therefore, nature can help us form our selfconcept, but if we identify as a nature person, we may be more likely to do activities to connect or interact with nature to fit our self-concept. In terms of research, understanding people's selfconcept can also help us distinguish between people (i.e. individual difference characteristics, such as nature relatedness, that create an individual's self-concept).

This differs from understanding nature relatedness as a merely descriptive individual difference characteristic; seeing it as part of the self-concept implies psychological processes of nature activities. By applying this to happiness, nature related people may be happier, in general, because they are doing nature activities that fit with their self-concept, such as seeking out and noticing nature more. These two ways of interacting or experiencing nature may not be exclusive, and may work alongside each other.
Are Nature Related Individuals More Likely to go Out into Nature?

People living in more urbanized environments may be less directly exposed to nature, or the nature they are exposed to may be different. Objectively, even if cities have a large degree of biodiversity in the city limits, people generally live in neighbourhoods with the least biodiversity (Turner et al., 2004). For example, city limits do not generally include forested areas, which may be viewed as quality nature, but may have access to marinas and greenspaces as natural areas.

This hints that when people visit more natural areas, it is usually internally motivated by choice or desire (Ajzen & Driver, 1991). This may suggest that individual difference characteristics, such as trait-like nature relatedness, predict individuals going out into nature.

When an individual responds to nature connection questionnaires, some items suggest that nature connected individuals are likely to go out into nature. For example, there are items in the Nature Relatedness scale (Nisbet et al., 2009) such as: "I enjoy being outdoors, even in unpleasant weather", "My ideal vacation spot would be a remote wilderness area", "I enjoy digging in the earth and getting dirt on my hands", "I don't often go out into nature" (reversecoded), and "The thought of being deep in the woods, away from civilization, is frightening" (reverse-coded; Nisbet et al., 2009); people who endorse these items from the experience subscale of the Nature Relatedness scale express that they are spending a lot of time in nature.

However, these self-report items are not directly assessing, objectively, if individuals high in nature relatedness are indeed more likely to go out into nature. As a broad self-report measure, it is important to corroborate face valid interpretations of the items against other indicators.

In general, research suggests that nature connected individuals are more likely to spend time in nature in different places around the world. Lin et al. (2014) examined the difference in an individual's nature orientation (i.e. nature relatedness) versus their opportunity (i.e. a person's access to the park) on self-report park use in Brisbane, Australia. Nature relatedness was a more important predictor for time spent in the parks and private nature spaces, such as gardens, than was easy access (i.e. opportunity) to these spaces. Further, nature related Australians were more willing to travel farther distances to find parks with a higher percentage of trees and native plant coverage (Shanahan et al., 2015b). In the UK, nature related individuals were more likely to frequent the local greenspaces (Flowers et al., 2016). In Tokyo, Japan, predicting the probability of greenspace use was highlighted by both factors of the landscape, but most importantly, with individuals' level of nature relatedness; furthermore, those with higher levels of nature relatedness were more likely to also report longer duration in urban greenspaces (Soga & Akasaka, 2019). French individuals who felt more connected to nature reported spending more time in natural places (Colléony et al., 2017). When asked which natural areas they were most likely to spend time in, nature connected French people were more likely to report both forests and urban parks than those lower in nature connection. My collaborators and I have also seen that during the COVID-19 pandemic, Canadian nature related students reported spending more time in nature (Desrochers et al., 2022). More specifically, nature relatedness was associated with more time spent in greenspaces, blue spaces, and countryside areas during a usual week of the pandemic. Additionally, when the participants were asked if they felt they were spending more or less time in nature during the pandemic than prior, nature related participants selfreported spending more time in all three natural environments, whereas the overall sample (i.e.
no matter their level of nature relatedness) reported spending about the same amount of time in nature during the pandemic than prior.

Moreover, nature related people spending more time in nature was also seen in more momentary assessments, such as daily diary or experience sampling data. These measurement techniques focus on concrete instances of behaviour, avoiding some biases stemming from general beliefs about the self. For example, in an experience sampling study, participants filled out a survey twice a week for eight weeks about the amount of time they spent outdoors and in nature over the previous three days. Here, trait nature relatedness was moderately associated with both time spent outdoors (r = .25) and in nature (r = .30; Nisbet et al., 2009). Similarly, in an unpublished daily diary study, where participants filled out a questionnaire every night about their day for 14 days, nature related people reported spending more time outdoors (Lutz, 2022).

In an unpublished experience sampling study, however, my collaborators and I have found that trait nature relatedness did not significantly predict time spent outdoors in experience sampling data measured three times a day for seven days in multilevel modelling analyses (Desrochers et al., 2021). This contradicts previous findings, although this data is highly positively skewed with a low average of how much time the student sample reported spending time outdoors (See Figure 1 for the distribution of responses). This skewed data may be missing out on the variability in the data needed to examine this relationship. The skewness of the data may be due to multiple different reasons. First, this data was collected during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in Ontario (fall 2020), where students were completing their classes virtually, and restrictions were in place, minimizing what they could do. However, the participants here were recruited during the same time as the participants from our lab's pandemic study (Desrochers et al., 2022), which showed a positive association between nature relatedness and time spent in nature. Second, we asked participants to report their time spent outdoors, not specifically in nature. This wording could affect the way the participants responded to this question. Third, it may be harder to gather momentary assessments of time spent outdoors versus daily reports (c.f. to Lutz, 2022). Even with this dataset's limitations, it suggests we may need better data on objective time spent in nature and nature relatedness.

The majority of the research proposes that nature-related individuals report spending more time in nature. Still, this line of research relies on self-report items of the time spent in nature. The little bit of research on more objective ratings of time spent in nature through experience sample measurements shows mixed results.
Are Nature Related Individuals more likely to Notice Nature?

Similar to being in nature, items in the Nature Relatedness scale (Nisbet et al., 2009) suggest nature-related individuals may be noticing more nature. These items are: "I take notice of wildlife wherever I am" (from the experience subscale) and "Even in the middle of the city, I notice nature around me" (from the Self subscale). People who report higher scores on these two items would suggest that they notice more nature; however, little research has directly examined this to date. Still, previous research may allude to this in indirect ways.

For one, previous research suggests that noticing nature is a way to connect people to nature, such as in the Five Pathways to connecting to nature (Lumber et al., 2017). The authors explored actions or activities a person can partake in to connect with nature. To figure out these activities, they examined which activities were done by people with high trait nature relatedness.

They found in two studies that trait nature relatedness was associated with doing more activities that engage with nature through the senses (contact), perceiving the aesthetic beauty of nature (beauty), using nature to express ideas or metaphors (meaning), feeling an emotional bond with nature (emotion), and feeling compassionate and ethical concern towards nature (compassion).

These five categories of activities were titled the Five Pathways to nature connection. The contact pathway includes activities such as seeing flowers, listening to birds, viewing beautiful sights, to name a few. These would be in line with noticing nature. However, it is not clear if these activities are happening while people go out into more remote natural areas or if they are happening in their everyday life. In the third study, the authors examined the Five Pathways as an intervention to see if the activities would indeed increase nature connection, as suggested from the previous studies. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three walking conditions: 1) walking in nature with pathway activities; 2) walking in nature without pathway activities; and 3) walking in an urban environment with pathway activities. The authors supported their hypothesis that nature relatedness was increased post activity from baseline scores, but this effect was only found for those in the nature walk with pathway activities condition (i.e. it was not significant in the built activity or the nature control conditions).

Further, other studies have also explored noticing nature explicitly as an intervention to increase state nature connection (noticing nature to nature relatedness causal direction). For example, having participants participate in a three good things in nature intervention (where they were to report three good things they noticed in their immediate environment) increased feelings of connection towards nature (Richardson & Scheffield., 2017). In this intervention, people generally described the good things as noticing nature through the senses, such as hearing birds chirp and seeing nature sights, similar to the contact through the senses pathway (Lumber et al., 2017). Experimentally, McEwan et al. (2019) showed that creating a noticing good things intervention in urban greenspaces was related to increased feelings of nature connectedness (operationalized through the Inclusion of Nature in Self scale and the Nature Relatedness scale).

For seven days, every time a participant was in the space they were randomly assigned to (either urban greenspace or urban built condition), they were prompted on a phone application to report one good thing they noticed in their immediate surrounding. Those in the greenspace condition were only prompted to report the one good thing when they were in a greenspace (and vice versa for urban built environment condition). After seven days of the intervention, the participants in both conditions saw an increase in nature connection scores from baseline values of nature relatedness and nature-self scores. This suggests that noticing good things increases feelings of nature connection no matter the environment. The authors suggest that the unexpected increase in nature connection for those in the built environment condition may come from people noticing nature even in those environments, or that being more mindful or aware of their surroundings may make them feel more connected to it. Additionally, Richardson et al. (2021) showed that noticing nature (measured through the frequency of doing nature noticing activities) was more important for predicting feelings of nature connectedness than solely spending time in nature.

Together, these studies show the association between noticing nature and nature relatedness. However, the direction of the association is mixed. In the experimental studies, the causal direction of the association shows that taking notice of nature through activities (e.

g. the Five Pathways and the good things) increases nature relatedness. It is unclear if nature related individuals are already noticing more nature than others (the reverse causal direction). The first two cross-sectional studies by Lumber et al. (2017) do suggest that trait nature related people report doing more noticing nature activities (which they then used to create the Pathways activities in the experimental study). Additionally, research showed that nature related individuals reported that they noticed more wildlife during the pandemic (Desrochers et al., 2022). These studies propose the reverse direction of the association between nature relatedness and noticing nature; however, it may be biased by self-report accounts. No studies have explored behavioural measures of noticing nature in this association. Noticing Nature Related to Well-Being One other purpose in exploring if nature related individuals are more likely to notice nature is to begin unpacking the process of noticing nature in everyday life as a way to feel happier. Research does suggest that those who notice nature see benefits of well-being because of it. The strongest claim to this is when Passmore & Holder (2016) asked participants to notice objects or scenes in daily life that evoked strong emotions over the course of two weeks. The participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: 1) a natural environment condition; 2) a human-built environment condition; or 3) a control condition. Those in the nature or human-built conditions were both told to notice the objects or scenes that evoked strong emotions, but they differed in telling them to notice in either natural or human-built environments. The control group was told to go about their regular life and were not instructed to notice anything. The authors found that when participants were asked to notice nature that evoked strong emotions, they reported more positive affect than those in the human-built and the control conditions. After the two-week noticing nature intervention, all participants were asked how much time they spent in nature during the intervention, regardless of condition.

Interestingly, there was no difference in the amount of time spent in nature during the two weeks between the conditions. This suggests that the individuals in the nature condition did not merely go out into nature more to be able to report noticing natural objects or scenes that evoked strong emotions. In other words, they noticed nature in their everyday lives, which increased their positive affect from pre-intervention levels. In qualitative data, those in the nature condition described more positive emotions evoked, whereas those in the human-built environment described more negative feelings. The natural object or environment itself generally evoked the descriptions of the strong emotions for those in the natural condition (e.g. "The two rainbows induced feelings of happiness and creativity. Seeing all the colours made me joyous and calm and peaceful." p. 542). In contrast, the strong emotions brought up in the human-built environment were more likely to bring up memories, be in light of activities, or discuss the functions of the object or scenes (e.g. "Jealous, envy, frustration, most emotions due to the fact I cannot afford a vehicle of that sort and see mostly younger individuals driving them." p. 542).
More recently, two replication studies have examined the noticing nature interventions.

In China, individuals who participated in the noticing nature intervention had more positive affect (replicating Passmore & Holder, 2016), life satisfaction, meaning in life, and transcendent connectedness, but also showed lower levels of stress, negative affect, and anxiety than those in either control condition (noticing urban condition and unrelated school journaling condition; Passmore et al., 2022a). These associations were not moderated by the participant's level of nature connectedness nor their time spent in nature. Passmore et al (2022b) also showed that the noticing nature intervention also worked in Canadian winter, where those noticing nature had higher levels of positive affect (replicating Passmore & Holder, 2016), life satisfaction, elevation, hope of agency, and state nature connection than those noticing built environments in urban spaces. Interestingly, in a post-intervention qualitative question asking participants if and what they had learned from the study, over-half of those in the urban condition mentioned nature. They suggested learning a greater affinity for natural settings, that paying attention to built objects made their appreciation for nature stronger, and more concern towards nature.

Altogether, these nature intervention studies highlight the benefit of showing people that taking notice of more nature may be more effective than just being in nature to connect with it and seeing emotional benefits from it.

Another study alludes to the relationship between noticing nature and well-being. For instance, when individuals reported one good thing they noticed in either greenspaces or urban environments, they reported more well-being, measured through better quality of life (measured with the Recovering Quality of Life scale; Keetharuth et al. 2018), positive affect, feelings of safety, and feelings of relaxation than baseline levels (McEwan et al., 2019). There was, however, no main effect of condition nor an interaction effect. This suggests that noticing (through the one good thing activity) was beneficial for the well-being markers regardless of the environment (urban or natural). This is similar to their results (McEwan et al., 2019) about noticing in either condition (urban or natural) on nature connection (see section Are Nature Related Individuals more likely to Notice Nature?). However, in this case, previous research on positive psychology interventions, such as the three good things, has been shown to improve feelings of gratitude and well-being. In this positive psychology research, the three good things activity is found to boost mood, no matter the location of the activity (Seligman et al., 2005).

Therefore, the lack of condition main effect or interaction effect for well-being is less surprising than the results on nature connection. Nisbet et al. (2019) examined the effects of nature exposure on moods and whether mindfulness instructions (i.e. guidance) during the nature exposure would increase the effect.

Participants were randomly assigned to an indoor walk, a nature walk, or a nature walk with mindfulness techniques. The nature walk and the nature walk with mindfulness techniques were taken on the same route (therefore, the same nature exposure). All three walks were guided by a research assistant. In the mindfulness condition, participants were instructed first to center their attention on the action of walking. Part of the way through the walk, the participants were then guided to focus their attention on a feature of their immediate surroundings, such as the sounds, the smells, or the sights. In other words, they were instructed to actively notice the surroundings (i.e. nature) through the senses. It was found that even though those in the nature walk reported fewer negative moods than those in the indoor walking condition, those in the mindfulness/noticing condition reported the least negative moods. In other words, the active engagement or noticing of the natural environment through the senses was more beneficial for reducing negative moods than solely the exposure to nature. However, the effect on positive mood was less clear. Those who walked outdoors (both with and without mindfulness) had better moods than those walking indoors, but the mindfulness technique did not significantly boost the effect more than the location. The mindfulness techniques did increase feelings of nature connection (measured through INS), similar to the other studies above.

Overall, there is a suggestion for the potential benefits of noticing nature. Even with the benefits shown for noticing nature on nature connection and well-being, it is not clear if trait nature relatedness would, in fact, predict noticing nature.

div.head: What is Noticing Nature?
div.p: Noticing is a colloquial term that could mean many different things. For example, the three definitions that come up from Oxford Languages Dictionary (n.d.) are: 1) "become aware of"; 2) "treat (someone) with some degree of attention or recognition"; and 3) "remark upon".

These definitions conclude that the term is about paying attention, perceiving, or explicitly acknowledging something or someone. Previously when discussing noticing nature, researchers have described this as paying attention to the nature around you and turning your senses to conscious thought. For example, Richardson et al. (2021) describe that when walking in an environment with nature, a person can be exposed to sensory information from natural stimuli, such as birds singing, smells of flowers, and sights of trees (to name a few). This is in accordance with Lumber et al.'s (2017) contact through the senses Pathways of nature connection.

Previously, Franco et al. (2017) reviewed the literature on the benefits of nature exposure through the senses with either explicit awareness of it or not. Many studies have shown that the benefits of nature can come without any awareness of the nature. As an illustration, an Ottawa study showed that individuals' self-reported neighbourhood satisfaction in general and satisfaction with the neighbourhood's nature were associated with the objective diversity of bird species of the neighbourhood (Hepburn et al., 2021). Interestingly, however, the residents who participated in the study did not seem aware of the bird diversity as a reason they felt satisfied with their area of residence (this was reported through open-ended questions). This suggests that merely having the biodiversity of nature (such as the birds) may be beneficial even if people cannot articulate the reasons. Other studies (some previously identified early) show that the objective measure of greenspace, greenness, or even access to nature is associated with wellbeing. In these studies, participants may still be aware of the nature exposure, but the assessment of nature is independent of their self-report. For example, in Glasgow et al.'s (2019) study, participants who travelled through more green or blue spaces had more positive moods. Green and blue spaces were assessed by GPS locations and motion-sensing data through the Daynamica phone application. Therefore, it is not clear if participants were aware or not of the environments that made them have more positive moods.

However, other studies rely on a person's self-report nature exposure (e.g. time spent in nature) and their well-being. These studies (many previously mentioned) depend on a person's awareness of nature. For example, White and colleagues (2019) had participants report how much time they spent outdoors, which they defined as natural areas outside of the city. To recall the time spent in these environments, the participants would have needed to notice the environments when they were being exposed to them. Due to this recalled awareness, there was an association between time spent in nature and life satisfaction. There is also research that examines more in-depth awareness (i.e. noticing of nature) and well-being. For instance, being mindful in nature spaces (Nisbet et al., 2019) and being aware of natural objects or scenes that cause strong emotions (Passmore & Holder, 2016;Passmore et al., 2022ab) are associated with well-being. Some researchers, such as Lumber et al. (2017) and Richardson et al. (2021), suggest that paying attention and using the senses is a way nature connected people may be immersing themselves in nature.

I believe it is important to examine more objective measures that align with the Nature Relatedness scale than solely relying on the self-report nature of the scale. As highlighted, the Nature Relatedness scale has items linked to spending time in nature and noticing nature.

Research has mostly supported the idea that nature related people spend more time in nature, though there are some method limitations. Even less research has examined if nature related individuals are indeed noticing more nature. This dissertation extends previous research by exploring subjective experience of noticing nature (i.e. consciously noticing nature). More specifically, I examined if nature related individuals do, in fact, consciously notice more nature, even when the objective circumstances are held constant across people. To do this, I did not specialize in one specific process that could define noticing nature, but instead, took a wider approach by examining two processes that fit the colloquial term. Behavioural measures were created to tap into the two processes of perception and attention. The goal was to create behavioural measures to explore noticing nature that is feasible for other researchers to use. The research was split into two phases: Phase 1 examined perception, and Phase 2 examined attention.

div.head: Perception
div.p: Phase 1 focused on examining the process of perception. In cognitive psychology, perception is defined as the conscious experience that comes from sensory information (Goldstein, 2011). For the purpose of the dissertation, I took a step further from this definition to also include some knowledge and judgement. Thus, when discussing perception, I mean a person's interpretation of nature. If a person does not define an object or scene as nature, they
will not recognize that they notice nature in an environment

. Not only is the definition of nature different across studies in the literature, but the perception of what counts as nature can also differ by individual people. Hartig and Kahn (2016) highlighted that "the term 'nature' means different things in different contexts. Recognizing personal and cultural aspects of the experience of nature, psychological research considers how different people encounter nature in diverse contexts, from viewing indoor plants in urban offices to walking in wilderness areas" (p. 936). Therefore, it is important to consider an individual's interpretation of what nature is when exploring if they are noticing everyday nature. This was taken into consideration by exploring the individual difference in what is perceived as nature in urban environments.

Previously, researchers have also discussed the potential of bottom-up versus top-down processing a person may use to characterize nature. Bottom-up processing of nature is defined by building the perception of nature based on sensory information from the external environment.

For example, Berman et al. (2014) explored low-level visual features of images of urban parks and natural scenery that were inferred to describe them as natural. Participants rated on a sevenpoint scale how unnatural/human-made (value of 1) to natural (value of 7) the scene in the image was, and the authors estimated low-level features of the images. The results suggest that images with fewer straight edges, more non-straight edges, and less colour saturation were reported as more natural (Berman et al., 2014). In this line of research, the low-level features are discovered by examining which features are associated with the naturalness ratings in the images. However, it may also suggest that these features are what a person uses in the image to create their rating of naturalness. Additionally, not only did the reported naturalness of the image predict a person's preference for the image, so did the similar low-level features that Berman et al. (2014) found (Kardan et al., 2015a). However, other research suggests that the semantics of nature is important for preference ratings. Kotabe et al. (2017) explored the nature-disorder paradox regarding ratings of aesthetic preferences for nature images (the same images used in Berman et al., 2014 andKardan et al., 2015a). More disorder in environments seems to reduce a person's preference for it, but natural environments, that are generally preferred, are also identified as disorderly. The researchers wanted to examine this paradox. They found that being able to fully picture the images in their original form (i.e. having semantics) instead of solely relying on low-level visual features was essential for the relationship between the level of naturalness with aesthetic preferences. In addition, the combination of low-level features (previously highlighted as inferring naturalness; Berman et al., 2014) and the semantics of the scene were essential to naturalness's influence on aesthetic preference over and above a natural image's self-report rating of disorder. This study exemplifies that bottom-up and top-down processing may both be used when characterizing nature and be important to nature's benefits.

Top-down processing is defined as the perception created by previous experience. Some research suggests that the benefits of nature come from using top-down processing to characterize nature. For example, when participants listened to pink noise (sound that is consistent in noise frequency for each octave interval), they were more likely to report the sound as pleasant, relaxing, and restorative if they were told the sound came from nature, compared to an industrial environment (Haga et al., 2016). Said another way, the benefit of nature was dependent on people's understanding of nature. Moreover, people had an aesthetic preference for nature sounds over urban sounds when easily distinguishable (Van Hedger et al., 2019). Hartig
