Even with a variation in what exactly is defined as nature or natural, there are key things that have a large consensus about what is considered nature. For example, in Figure 2, animals, flowers, and trees have a high frequency of being highlighted as nature in both groups. Other research shows that people define nature as undisturbed by humans and separate from civilization (Fehnker et al., 2021;Haluza-DeLay, 2001;Pointon, 2014;Vining et al., 2008). In this phase, I explored if nature related individuals perceive a broader range of features as nature in an urban setting.

div.head: Attention
div.p: Phase 2 explored the process of attention. As a social psychologist with limited expertise in cognitive psychology, I wanted to explore a more colloquial definition of the term attention than what cognitive psychologists have defined as the cognitive process of attention. As defined by the Oxford Dictionary (n.d.), the colloquial definition of attention is taking notice of, being aware, or consciously observing something or someone. These definitional terms of attention relate to what cognitive researchers consider explicit processing of attention, where there is a conscious processing of the information.
For the purpose of the dissertation, I focused on how natural objects in a scene of primarily urban/non-natural scenes draw and sustain participants' preferred attention.

Specifically, I explored where the eyes are being drawn to and what a person wants to focus on in an urban setting. I labelled these two "processes" of attention as first attention (where the eyes were being drawn) and voluntary attention (where the participant wanted to focus their attention). My definition of voluntary attention is quite different from the one used by cognitive psychologists. Voluntary (selective or endogenous) attention is defined in cognitive psychology as conscious attention driven by the individual towards the stimuli (Goldstein, 2011). In other words, the attention is a top-down processing (the mind intentionally focuses on the stimuli).

Much of the research on attention and natural environments fits within the Attention Restoration Theory. In this theory, the features of nature make it softly fascinating, enabling involuntary attention (defined as attention that requires little to no effort to focus on; Kaplan & Berman, 2010). This soft fascination allows people to not focus solely on nature but also on other thoughts (i.e., allowing the mind to wander), making it restorative from the hard fascinations in one's life. In this research, nature reduces feelings of fatigue and helps regain attentional capacity. For example, many research studies examine the benefits of nature on attention control in laboratory attention tasks (Basu et al., 2019;Gamble et al., 2014;Berman et al., 2008;Stenfors et al., 2019). This line of research is in light of cognitive psychology's definition of attention. However, little to no research has examined the attention as the focus being paid towards nature.
The limited research on paying attention to nature has utilized eye-tracking techniques.

Some eye-tracking research suggests that individual difference characteristics can differentiate between fixation points for natural environments. For example, students majoring in forestry were more likely to fixate on natural images, like forests and wetlands; in contrast, art students were more likely to fixate on images of humanistic attributes, such as urban and recreational areas (Wang et al., 2021). This suggests that an individual who may be more familiar or comfortable with the surroundings may pay more attention to it. Said another way, this could indicate that a person may be looking at objects or scenes that fit within their self-concept.

A single study has examined the difference in voluntary attention being paid to nature for people with varying degrees of nature relatedness through eye-tracking techniques. Bingjing et al. (2022) recorded the eye movement and fixation of participants wearing virtual reality headsets, with half of the scene set in an urban setting and half in a natural environment. The 360 ° virtual reality consisted of 180 °of buildings (built/urban environment) and 180 °of trees (natural environment). Individuals with high levels of nature relatedness (top 31% of the sample) spent more time looking at the natural environment, whereas those low in nature relatedness (bottom 33% of the sample) spent more time looking at the urban setting. There was no difference in the time spent looking at natural or urban settings for those with a medium level of nature relatedness (middle 36% of the sample). There was also a significant association between high nature relatedness and time spent looking at trees. This is the first study to directly examine how nature related individuals were objectively more likely to focus their attention on nature.

However, this study does not consider the subjective awareness of their noticing. By this, I mean that the participants may subconsciously spend more time looking at nature, but they may not be aware they are doing this. Additionally, this study had an equal amount of natural and urban stimuli in the study. This may suggest that nature related individuals are purposely exposing themselves to the natural setting more than the urban one, but it does not consider noticing nature elements within the urban part of the environment.

div.head: The Current Studies
div.p: The current dissertation explores whether nature-related individuals notice more nature.

To do this, I examined how an individuals' level of trait nature relatedness relates to two processes I deemed essential for exploring behavourial noticing of nature in one's life. To accomplish this, I ran three studies in two separate phases. Phase 1 focused on the process of perception, defined as the interpretation of what is nature. Phase 2 focused on the process of attention, described as focus being drawn to or being held by nature. In all three studies, to control for the level of naturalness, images of urban scenes with a degree of nature were used.

This way, all participants were exposed to the same amount of nature, but I predicted that some would perceive or pay attention to the nature in the scenes more than others. Across both Phases, I hypothesized that highly nature related people would be likely to notice more nature.

In Phase 1, participants were exposed to many images of urban scenes with a degree of nature. To explore the perception of nature, the participants reported if they notice the nature in the image by rating how much nature they see in the urban space and by rating the percentage of nature in the images. This phase explored how nature relatedness may be associated with nature perception (if they notice the nature or not). I hypothesized (H1) a positive association with nature relatedness and each nature perception item, where those higher in nature relatedness would be more likely to report that they perceived more nature in the urban environment images.

In Phase 2, to explore attention to nature, the participants were also exposed to many images with an urban scene containing some nature. The participants were asked to report on two attention questions for each image. First, participants were asked to indicate where their attention was drawn to the image. Second, participants were requested to indicate where they would like to focus their attention on in the image. I hypothesized that those higher in nature relatedness would be more likely to pay attention to nature. More specifically, when examining an urban scene, I hypothesized (H2) a positive association between nature relatedness and first attention, where those with higher levels of nature relatedness would be more likely to have their attention drawn toward the little bit of nature in the image; I also hypothesized (H3) a positive association between nature relatedness and voluntary attention, where those with higher levels of nature relatedness would be more likely to want to focus their attention on the nature in the image. This fits with research on eye-tracking techniques.

However, eye-tracking techniques consider unconscious attention on the natural environment, such as in Bingjing et al.'s (2022) study. In this dissertation, I focused on conscious attention (i.e., the participants being aware that they are paying attention to the nature by asking the participants to report on where they focused their attention first and where they want to focus it). Altogether, this dissertation investigated if nature relatedness was associated with the subjective noticing of nature through two phases with three hypotheses. To accomplish this, I developed new tasks to measure behavioural indicators of noticing nature. Previous research relied on self-report measures of time spent in nature or activities related to noticing nature, which lacked objectivity. By assessing noticing through these novel tasks, I extended this line of research by examining if the self-report responses align with the behaviour of noticing nature. Thus, with the creation of new behavioural tasks of noticing nature, another goal of the dissertation was the tool development. It was crucial to properly evaluate the new tasks, as any negative results could be attributed to poor task design rather than a lack of effect. Further, with the proper tool development, other researchers may use the task to explore similar relationships. An Open Science Framework (OSF) database was created to provide readers with preregistrations, materials, syntaxes, and other relevant information for the current studies: https://osf.io/hcdp2/?view_only=b2ef552766df41f9aa7b221827cac9bf . Phase 1 Study 1 Study 1 explores if individuals high in nature relatedness perceive nature in images
portraying urban scenes with some nature. To do this, I designed two tasks of nature perception.

Before examining the hypothesized relationship between nature relatedness and nature perception, it is important to assess the reliability of the experimental tools (i.e. the two nature perception item-types). If there is not a proper distribution for each image, it would be hard to aggregate all images reliably, and it would also be hard to explore further relationships (see review by Clark, 1995). That is, if there is not enough between-people variability in the image ratings, it will be hard to examine if nature relatedness predicts the nature perceptions. Said another way, if everyone either notices or does not notice the nature in the images (regardless of their nature relatedness levels), then it will not allow me to investigate the correlation between nature relatedness and the nature perceptions of the images. Therefore, I employed optional stopping techniques to stop my recruitment at 100 participants to allow me to test the variability of the nature perception ratings of the images. After properly assessing the variability of my tools, I continued recruitment until I reach 300 participants before running more psychometric analyses to optimize my experimental tools. Lastly, after the best images and item(s) were chosen, the correlations between nature relatedness and nature perceptions were assessed.

div.head: Methods
div.p: Participants. Due to the study's exploratory features, it is difficult to properly choose a likely effect size or the smallest effect size of interest to run an a priori power analysis.

However, it is still essential to justify the required sample size. In addition, it is important to have good power to allow for exploration (Lakens, 2022). A previous simulation study has indicated that correlations generally stabilize with a sample of at least 250 individuals for a small effect size of .1 with 80% confidence (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013). Therefore, a sample size of 300 will be run to allow for the deletion of poor data. A sensitivity analysis was run in G*Power to explore the effect size that can be identified with this sample size. With alpha set at .05, 90%
power, and a sample size of 250, an effect size of as small as .12, regardless of direction, can be identified.

Three hundred participants were recruited. Ten participants did not complete the study (36% or less completion rate) and thus, were removed from the sample. After identifying the problematic participants through outliers and string responding, the final sample was 282

(𝑀 𝑎𝑔𝑒 = 20.44, 𝑆𝐷 = 4.41, min = 17, max = 49). Out of the eight participants who were removed: one was removed for being identified as an outlier for nature relatedness (±3 standard deviations away from the mean), four for having no variability in the image ratings for item 1 (i.e. string responding), and six for having no variance in their nature relatedness responses (i.e.
string responding).

For the final sample of 282, 197 identified their gender as women (70%), 67 identified it as man (24%), 13 identified as gender fluid/non-binary/two-spirited (5%), one identified as a trans-man (<1%), one as a non-binary trans-femme (<1%), one preferred not to say (<1%), and two did not respond to the question (<1%). The majority of the sample identified as White (61%), with a smaller percentage of South Asian (11%), Chinese (9%), Black (8%), Arab (5%), Indigenous (3%), West Asian (2%), Southeast Asian (1%), Filipino (1%), Latin American (1%), Korean (<1%), Japanese (<1%), other (3%), and 3% preferred not to identify their ethnicity. The majority of participants grew up and currently lived in the suburbs (see the frequency of each area in Table 1). The majority of participants filled out the questionnaire on laptops/desktops (90%), with a smaller percentage on phones (5%) and tablets (4%). See Appendix A for all the items collected.

div.head: Measures.
div.p: Perceived Nature. To assess individuals' perceptions of nature in urban images, two different question types were asked:

1) "Rate how much nature you perceive in this urban scene?". The participants rated this item on a 7-point scale anchored from 1 = there is no nature for an urban scene to 7 = there is a lot of nature for an urban scene. This item is identified as the 7-point scale rating item.
2) "What percentage of the image is nature?". The participant responded to this question from 0 (no nature at all) to 100 (all nature) to allow for variability in the rating of nature.
This item is identified as the percentage rating item.

Nature Relatedness. The Nature Relatedness scale (NRS; Nisbet et al., 2009) was used to measure a person's feeling of nature connectedness. This scale consists of 21-items examining three subscales: Self (nine items), Experience (six items), and Perspective (six items). The Self subscale examines an individual's intrapersonal feelings towards connecting and feeling a part of nature; the Experience subscale explores experiential moments, noticing, and attention in nature;

and the Perspective subscale measures attitudes toward nature worldviews. Each item was rated on a Likert-type scale from 1 = disagree strongly to 5 = agree strongly. I computed the average score for each subscale (Experience ∝ = .76; Self ∝ = .83; Perspectives ∝ = .59) and an overall NRS score (across all 21-items; ∝ = .83). Additionally, the items "Even in the middle of the city, I notice nature around me" and "I take notice of wildlife wherever I am" of the NRS were used as individual face valid items of noticing nature.

div.head: SPANE.
div.p: As an extra analysis, not pre-registered in my prospectus, I wanted to also examine positive and negative affect.

This measure was added because it aligns with my reasoning behind the goal of my dissertation. One of my suggested reasons for examining if nature related individuals were more likely to perceive nature in my dissertation was to examine if this was a potential reason why nature related individuals were happier in general. I, therefore, measured affect through the Scale of Positive and Negative Experience (SPANE; Diener et al., 2010). The scale contains 12 items, with six items about positive emotions and six negative emotions. The participants were asked to rate how often they experienced each of the 12 emotions in the last four weeks. Average scores were created for positive affect (PA; ∝ = .87) and negative affect (NA; ∝ = .83). Three items were added ad-hoc from SPANE to measure feelings of awe. These three items were awe, wonder, and amazement. An average across all three items was computed (∝ = .82). Noticing Nature Activities. An additional extra measure I added outside of my pre-registered prospectus was to test a face valid noticing nature measure. To do this, the Noticing Nature Activities (NNA; Richardson et al., 2021) scale was measured. Richardson and colleagues (2021) defined noticing nature as actively paying attention and engaging with the sensory information from nature and bringing "elements of attention, awareness, and intention" (p. 2) to it (i.e. bringing it to mind). The NNA is a 13-item scale asked participants to indicate how often they did each of the noticing nature activities, on a 4-point scale (1 = Never to 4 = Often). An average of how frequent participants did all 13 activities was computed (∝ = .87). An example noticing nature activity is "taken time to notice butterflies and/or bees". This face valid measure allows me to see if an individual who is self-reporting doing noticing nature activities in their real-life (i.e. higher score on the NNA scale) also reports perceiving more nature with my nature perception items I created.

div.head: Materials.
div.p: Images. Participants were exposed to 50 images for each nature perception item-type.

The decision to use 50 images came from the consideration of wanting to have a large number of images to have higher reliability when aggregating the image ratings into a single score, but not wanting to make the task too tedious for the participants by exposing them to too many images. I came to my conclusion by examining how many images and item ratings previous research used with nature/urban images (full details on this decision can be seen in my pre-registration on OSF).
The 50 images portrayed urban scenes, but include some degree of nature. The nature in the urban scenes were plants, flowers, animals, birds, water, and/or mountains (to name a few).

The images vary in the amount of nature in the images. See Figure 3 for example images (all images can be seen on OSF). The images were labelled with number IDs to help identify the images for the psychometric analyses.

div.head: Psychometric Analysis Results: Assessing the Experimental Tools
div.p: At 100 participants, across both item-types, there were eight images identified as potentially problematic (see Appendix B for a full report on the psychometric analysis results for the sample of 100 participants). Seven images were left-skewed with low means for both items, whereas one was right-skewed with a large mean. These eight images, however, had appropriate standard deviation (7-point scale rating item: between 0.99 and 1.43; percentage rating item: between 11.16 to 20.32) and a good range of values (7-point scale rating item: smallest range 1 to 5; percentage rating item: smallest range 30 to 100). Overall, the initial set of 50 images were acceptable to continue using, thus, a full sample (N ~ 300) was recruited to explore their variability and potentially use them to examine the association with nature relatedness.

After recruiting 300 participants and data cleaning (see details in the Participants section of Study 1 Methods), a second round of psychometric analyses was performed. Similar to the first round of psychometric analyses, the variability of how much nature the participants perceived in the urban scene images was assessed through the descriptive statistics of the distribution, a visual assessment of the distribution, reliability analyses, and inter-image correlations. Additionally, before running the main analysis, multilevel models were examined to explore if there was substantial between-participants variability in the ratings across the images and not solely within-participant variability. Lastly, principal component analyses and individual correlations between each image and nature relatedness were explored to choose the best images to aggregate.

div.head: 7-Point Scale Rating
div.p: Item -"Rate how much nature you perceive in this urban scene?". For the total sample, the average rating of nature perception across all 50 images was 3.68 (SD = 1.00), which is close to the middle value of the scale (4) and similar to the mean across all images for the psychometric analyses at 100 participants (M = 3.67). Descriptive statistics for each individual image can be seen in Table 2. The minimum mean rating of nature perception was 1.86 (Image 30), and the maximum mean was 6.45 (Image 23). The preregistered criterion for the mean was to be around the middle value of the scale, which is 4.

There were 13 images with means below the value of 3 and five above the value of 5. The visual representation of the distributions for each image can be seen in Figure 4. Aggregating all the images together showed good reliability, Cronbach's ∝ = .96, Omega = .95, and split-half reliability r(280) = .91 p < .001, 95% CI [.88, .93]. The reliability, through Cronbach's ∝, was robust from removing each individual image (all images showed either a decrease or no change in ∝ if removed), indicating that this was not an appropriate criterion to use when examining the variability of the images. The range of inter-image correlations was from r = -.22 to r = .64.

There were 11 images that had some negative correlations with other images (Images 2,3,6,10,11,21,23,30,41,43,& 46). Next, an unconditional multilevel model was run to explore if there was enough betweenparticipants variability in the ratings of the 7-point scale rating item. To do this, the data was nested within individual participants. The intraclass correlation (ICC) of the unconditional model indicated that 18.99% of the data variance is due to the within-person effect. This percentage indicates that there is a portion of the variance due to the variation in the image (i.e. an individual person varied in their ratings for the different images), but that there is still enough betweenparticipants variability to explore the individual difference characteristic nature relatedness. This within-person variability may suggest that the variation in the rating is due to the differences in urban images because each image has a different degree of nature.

Overall, the psychometric analyses suggest the images have decent variability to aggregate for the association. However, prior to aggregating the images, I also looked at ways to identify the best images to aggregate for the hypothesized correlation. First, a principle components analysis (PCA) was explored. Images were vetted as appropriate for PCA by exploring inter-image correlations before running the PCA. A detailed description of the PCA results can be seen in Appendix C. Forty-four images were deemed suitable for PCA (Images 3,10,21,23,30,& 46 were deemed unsuitable for PCA). A single-factor solution was identified as the best suited for the observed responses. Three additional items (Images 8, 9, & 43) showed higher factor loadings on other factors (with small Eigenvalues) and were therefore suggested to be removed. The reliability of the 41 images was identified as good, but reduced slightly from the reliability of the full set of images: Cronbach's ∝ = .95, Omega = .95 95% CI [.94, .96], split-half reliability r(280) = .90 p < .001 95% CI [.88, .93].

Additionally, I also explored the correlation between nature relatedness and each of the individual images ratings. The majority of images were not significantly correlated with nature relatedness. A single correlation was significant; Image 24 had a significant correlation, r(278) = .13 p = .04. (Note that 2.5 significant correlations would be expected by chance under the null.) There were 31 images with non-significant positive correlations, 17 with non-significant negative correlations, and 1 with a correlation of 0. The average correlation between each image and nature relatedness was z = .02 (as computed with Fisher's r-to-z transformed correlations).

The range of correlations was between r = -.10 (Image 25) and r = .13 (Image 24). When splitting the data into the images with a negative correlation and positive correlation, the average of the 31 images with a positive correlation (not including the correlations of 0) was z = .04, and the average of the other 15 images with a negative correlation was z = -.03.

div.head: Percentage Rating Item -What percentage of nature do you perceive?
div.p: The quantitative values of these analyses can be viewed in Table 3, and the histograms for each image can be seen in Figure 5. The variability of the images was compared to the value across all the images. The mean value of nature perception was 35.94% (SD = 15.57%). This mean value is similar to the mean identified at 100 participants (M = 35.74). The minimum mean percentage was 12.31% (Image 30) and the maximum was 81.32% (Image 23). The reliability across all 50 images was good, Cronbach's ∝ = .96, Omega = .96, and spit half-reliability r(279) = .91 p < .001, 95% CI [.88, .94]. The reliability estimates were also robust in removing each image (all images showed either a decrease or no change in ∝ if removed). div.head: Discussion
div.p: In Phase 1 of the dissertation, I wanted to explore if nature related individuals would notice more nature through the process of perception. I asked participants to rate 50 images on how much nature they perceived with a 7-point scale and a percentage rating. Due to the toolbuilding nature of the study, I ran psychometric analyses to ascertain the extent of the variability among images to allow the exploration of the association with nature relatedness. Across the initial sample of 100 participants and the final sample of 284 participants, the images showed reasonable variability through descriptive statistics, reliability analyses (Cronbach's alpha, Omega, and split-half reliability), and inter-image correlations. Further, MLM results indicated that the images had enough between-person variability to explore an association between an individual difference characteristic and the image ratings. Lastly, principal component analyses and individual correlations with nature relatedness were run to identify the best images to use when aggregating the two nature perception item-types prior to data analysis. Despite reasonable variability, links with trait nature relatedness did not emerge. More specifically, when looking at both individual images and aggregated means of nature perception item-types across all images, a null association with nature relatedness was evinced. Additionally, this null association was robust across the exploration of different sets of images, identified through the psychometric analyses. This suggests that, with my current tools, nature related individuals do not, in fact, notice more nature, through perception, in urban environment photos than those low on nature relatedness. Therefore, the results did not support H1.

It is unclear with this single study whether the results suggest a lack of nature perception differences across the nature relatedness dimension, or if the research tool I built did not accurately measure the concept of nature perception (or noticing nature, in general). Though psychometric analyses suggested the items were, in fact, measuring something reliably and that there was enough between-person variability in the ratings between the images, the tool I created may have been measuring something outside of noticing nature. For one, there was no association between more face-valid noticing nature items and the items of nature perception.

The face valid items from the NRS ("Even in the middle of the city, I notice nature around me" and "I take notice of wildlife wherever I am") and the Noticing Nature Activities scale (Richardson et al., 2021) were added to explore the validity of my newly created tool for measuring noticing nature. This lack of correlation between these face-valid measures and my nature perception items indicates that the tool may explore something different than noticing nature. In other words, nature perception (or whatever this task measures) may differ from the concept of noticing nature.

There remains some uncertainty about what the perception task is assessing, yet it may still be measuring participants' perception of how much nature is in the images. A key driver of differences in nature perceptions may be differences in participants' definitions of nature; for example, (how much) is a potted plant actually nature? The individual differences (as identified through reliability and the MLM results) in these responses could highlight that the conceptualization of nature differs across people and contexts (Hartig & Kahn, 2016). In other words, the conceptualization of nature may come more from top-down processing (Haga et al., 2016;Van Hedger et al., 2019;Hartig et al., 2014) than bottom-up processing, as suggested by research on low-level features of nature (Berman et al., 2014;Kardan et al., 2015a;Kotabe et al., 2017).
However, little research has examined, generally, what people conceptualize as nature.

From the minimal work, the main themes identify nature is separate from or untouched by humans (Fehnker et al., 2021;Vining et al., 2008) and "out there" away from civilization (Haluza-Delay, 2001;Wilson, 2019). This suggests that the context of an urban environment may reduce a person's perception of nature within it.

Some studies suggest that differences in conceptualizations of nature may be due to a person's levels of nature relatedness. An unpublished study by a previous Happiness Lab graduate student Dan Shaw (2018) asked participants to identify key features of nature in three minutes. Results showed that not only did those high in nature relatedness identify substantially more features than those low in nature relatedness (see Figure 1), but they also differed on their ratings of prototypicality (i.e. a rating of how characteristic the term was to natural environment) of 100 of the most frequent features of natural environments. Those higher in nature relatedness reported the features, in general, as higher in prototypicality. This was also the case across the level of prototypicality (splitting the terms into high, medium, and low prototypicality based on average scores across all participants). Together, this may suggest that nature related individuals may have a richer language for nature and that they have more strong feelings towards what is nature.

Although the conceptualization of nature and its differences by people (level of nature relatedness) may be one part at play for perception, it is most likely not the whole picture. There may be other biases that influence the understanding of perception. For example, where a participant focuses their attention may also influence their response to nature perception. If

Participant A focused their attention on the tree in the background of the image, whereas Participant B focused their attention on the car that drove by the tree, participant A might have rated perceiving more nature than Participant B. This other potential aspect of noticing nature (attention) will be explored in Phase 2 of the dissertation.

Other biases to perception may be how much weight participants put on the urban context of the images reducing the perception of nature. This abstract weight to the responses may be influenced by a participant's level of nature relatedness. In a study by a previous undergrad thesis student from the Happiness lab, Tristan Marshall (2022) asked participants to rate how representative 137 images, that fit into seven categories (green wilderness, arid wilderness, urban, people in nature, nature in urban areas, expansive nature, and nature as utility), were to their concept of either nature or natural environment. Marshall (2022) found some differences in the "perception" of natural environments by levels of nature relatedness. For the image category most similar to my images (e.g. urban greenspaces, tree-lined neighbourhoods), there was a difference in the conceptualization fit where highly nature related individuals reported that images were less representative of their concept of nature/natural environments. There was also a similar difference for urban images with little to no greenery and images of nature that were viewed as more utilitarian (e.g. agriculture and natural resources). However, there was no association between nature relatedness and image categories with more nature (humanity included nature, expansive nature, arid nature, and wilderness). Even though nature related individuals felt some aspects of nature were more characteristic of a natural environment (i.e. the prototype study), including the context of urban environments may influence natural features to be perceived as less natural due to the context (i.e. the photo study). In other words, two competing processes (i.e., highly nature related people often defining more things as nature, but less so in urban contexts) may combine to create a null association in the perception task here.

One significant association found in the study was between the 7-point scale nature item and affect. More specifically, when participants reported noticing more nature in the urban environment images, they also reported feeling more positive affect in the last four months. This is interesting as the proposed hypothesis of nature related individuals noticing more nature stemmed from research showing that nature related individuals were happier people in general (Capaldi et al., 2014;Pritchard et al., 2020) and that happiness may be found through being in contact with nature (McMahan & Estes, 2015) and also noticing it (Passmore & Holder, 2016;Passmore et al., 2022ab). In the current study, nature related individuals did report more positive affect, and even though nature relatedness was not associated with nature perception, affect was associated with nature perception. This may still suggest that nature related individuals, when asked to perceive nature in urban environments, report not noticing more because of their high threshold for what constitutes nature there, but maybe do, still, notice it in their everyday life.
Once more, this suggests that my new tool may not be an accurate way of assessing noticing nature through the process of perception.

Altogether, the findings of this phase suggest a null association between nature relatedness and nature perception. This may stem from the urban context of the images reducing the perception of nature, or it may be that the perception items were not appropriate measures for noticing nature. Nevertheless, due to this null association, a replication study was not run with Amazon Mechanical Turk employees.

div.head: Phase 2
div.p: Phase 2 explores the process of attention. Attention, here, is defined as what an individual notices first in a conscious way (first attention) and what in the image they want to focus their attention on more (voluntary attention). I hypothesized that an individual high on trait nature relatedness would notice nature first in an urban scene image more often and that they would want to focus on the nature more. This phase was run simultaneously to Phase 1. NRS. String responding is defined as participants responding in the same manner across items of the NRS. div.head: Psychometric Analyses Results
div.p: Three rounds of optional stopping and psychometric analyses were performed before a set of 50 images with appropriate variability was found. For every round, 100 participants were recruited and psychometric analyses were run to test the variability of each item. For both items separately, the variability for each image was tested by examining descriptive statistics (such as minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, and frequency of the area clicked), a standardized distribution of the images created with Z-transformed mean scores for each image

2 , reliability analysis, and inter-image correlations. These analyses identified a set of unsuitable images. These unsuitable images were replaced, and a new sample of 100 participants was recruited. During Round 1, 32 images were deemed unsuitable and needed to be replaced. During Round 2, 11 images needed replacing. During Round 3, the images demonstrated appropriate variability to continue recruitment to the full sample size of 300. More details for each round can be found in Appendix E. The same psychometric analyses, and a few extra, were examined for each nature attention item separately during the fourth round (i.e. full sample).

First Attention. All quantitative results of the psychometric analyses for the first attention item can be seen in Table 7. Approximately 32% of all the clicks were on the nature areas. The percentage of nature clicks did vary across images with a range of 2% (Image 70) to 93% (Image 85). The mean of 0.32 is the largest mean across all psychometric rounds, but relatively similar in size. Additionally, all images showed some variance in the responses (i.e. no image had 0 participants clicking the nature area). The range of inter-image correlations was from r = -.26 to r = .38. All images had a minimum of six negative correlations with other images (i.e. negative inter-image correlations). 2 The Z-scores were created for each image in comparison to the overall mean across all the images, thereby, allowing the comparison of means across the different images. The 50 images showed good reliability, Cronbach's ∝ = .70, which was an improvement from Round 3 (∝ = .67). The reliability was quite robust to the removal of the individual images.

The majority of images (42 images) were identified as good (i.e. Cronbach's ∝ was reduced when the image was removed) with a change range of .001 to .02. Seven images (2, 46, 52, 59, 64, 74 & 88) were considered poor to aggregate because the reliability score was increased when removing each individually, with a maximum increase of Cronbach's ∝ of .01. A single image showed no change in Cronbach's ∝ when removed (Image 7). When running other measures of reliability, such as split-half reliability and Omega, the reliability was identified to be low, splithalf reliability, r(291) = .52 p < .001 95% CI [.42, .61], Omega = .65.
The standardized distribution of the Z-transformed means for each image was examined.

The distribution of all 50 images was right-skewed (see Figure 7) and identified as non-normal (Table 8). The robustness of the distribution was examined by removing the images with the lowest percentage of nature clicks. Four robustness tests were run: 1) removing images with 5% or less nature clicks; 2) removing the images with 10% or less nature clicks; 3) removing images with 15% or less nature clicks; and 4) removing images with 20% or less nature clicks. The distribution did not become normal after removing the images for each robustness test (see Table 8). Additionally, outliers were identified (approximate +3SD above mean, more specifically above the value of 2.7), and thus, the normality robustness tests were re-run without these outliers. The distribution became statistically normal after removing the outliers from the full sample of 50 images. A visual of this distribution with 47 images can be seen in Figure 8. div.head: Statistical Analysis Results: Correlations with Nature Attention Items
div.p: The pre-registered data analysis plan to test the hypotheses was to examine bivariate correlational analyses between the aggregates of the 50 images for each attention item and nature relatedness; however, similar to Study 1, the psychometric analysis results may suggest better images to aggregate. Thus, the robustness of the correlations between the two attention items and nature relatedness was explored. There were four different combinations of image sets computed and examined. For each set, there was a separate set created for each item. The first set was the complete set of 50 images (Table 11i). The second sets were created with only the images identified as suitable for distribution (Table 11ii). The third sets were created with only the images identified as suitable for reliability (Table 11iii). Lastly, the fourth sets were created with only images positively correlated with nature relatedness (Table 11iv). A description of the different sets can be seen in Table 11. Note: For voluntary attention, there were no images identified through psychometric analyses to remove for the distribution criteria. Thus, this image set were disregarded for voluntary attention task.

The different aggregate sets were then correlated with nature relatedness. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals were run for these correlations with 1000 sample Bootstrapping. All statistical analysis results can be seen in Table 12. The correlations between nature relatedness and both nature attention tasks were significant. This pattern was also seen across the other aggregated images (i.e. the correlation was robust across different sets of images). Thus, hypotheses 2 and 3 were supported, suggesting that nature related individuals are more likely to notice nature first and want to focus their attention on nature in an urban scene image.

More exploratory correlations were also explored, in addition to the main correlations between nature relatedness and each attention item. The exploratory correlations were between the two nature attention items with affect (positive, negative, and awe), noticing nature activity, the nature relatedness subscales and the two individual items that were face valid to my research hypothesis (item 8: "Even in the middle of the city, I notice nature around me" and item 21: "I take notice of wildlife wherever I am").

The association of nature relatedness with the two attention items was the strongest and most robust for the Self subscale of the NRS. The significant correlations of voluntary attention with both Perspective and Experience subscales of NRS were robust across the different sets.

The Experience subscale was consistently not significantly associated with first attention across the different sets, whereas there were more mixed results for the correlation of the Perspective subscale and first attention. It (the Perspective subscale) was significant at the overall level (Table 12i) and with the images positively correlated to nature relatedness (Table 12iv); however, it was not significant for the other two image sets: images that fit a normal distribution (Table 12ii) and images deemed good for reliability (Table 12iii).

For the face-valid noticing nature items and measures (NRS Items 8 & 21; NNA), there was a consistent positive correlation between first attention and voluntary attention with NNA across all sets of images. Less consistency was seen for the two NRS items. Both NRS items were positively correlated with voluntary attention. In contrast, item 8 was correlated with the first attention task at the overall level (Table 12i) and for image sets with only positively correlated to nature relatedness images (Table 12iv), whereas item 21 was only correlated with the last set (Table 12iv).
Positive affect was not significantly associated with either attention item across all sets.

There was a consistent significant positive association with negative affect for the first attention item; the affect associations with voluntary attention were all consistently non-significant. correlation (r = .12), the sampling size of approximately 300 participants may also increase sampling error and reduce the correlation's accuracy. To strive for more reliability in the robustness of the correlations and validity of the measurement tool, running a replication study with a larger and different sample is important. Thus, to further explore the significant associations, a replication study was run to try to confirm the results from this study. This allows consideration of the consistency of the results in a different sample of community members in Canada and the United States.

div.head: Participants.
div.p: To justify the sample of Study 3, using the information from Schönbrodt and Perugini's (2013) simulation, a sample of at least 470 is needed for the most stable correlation (smallest width of stability) for a small effect size of .10 with 95% confidence (this is higher confidence than for Study 2). A sensitivity analysis was run with G*Power to explore the smallest effect size that can be detected with this sample size. With an alpha set to .05, power set to 90%, and a sample size of 470, an effect size of .09, regardless of direction, can be detected.

Differently from Study 2, participants were only exposed to one of the two attention tasks. This was chosen to shorten the participation time for each participant, and it helps ensure that the results for voluntary attention do not depend on the initial task. Because of this, I needed to double my sample size to ensure an appropriate sample size was used to explore the association of each attention item with nature relatedness. Therefore, the target sample size was 1100 (i.e. a sample of 550 participants for each attention task). This sample size will also allow for the deletion of some poor data.

A sample of 1128 participants was recruited. As pre-registered, participants were excluded if they: 1) did not complete the study survey (n = 63), 2) were identified as an outlier on the NRS (n = 5), 3) demonstrated string responding on the NRS items (n = 3), and/or 4) responded that they could not commit quality to their responses (n = 6). A total of 76 participants were removed 4 . div.head: Discussion
div.p: Study 3 aimed to replicate the findings from Study 2, which found that nature related individuals were more likely to notice nature in urban environments through the process of attention. A replication study was conducted to evaluate the generalizability and robustness of the results in a larger sample outside of the convenient recruitment of university students. Over 1100 Amazon Mturk workers were recruited through Cloud Research to participate in the study.

The participants were randomly assigned to the first attention or voluntary attention task before completing the same questionnaire measures as Study 2. Psychometric analysis results provided that the images had enough variability to explore the association of the individual difference characteristic of nature relatedness with each of the attention items. Overall, the results of the current study did replicate results from Study 2. Thus, nature related individuals were more likely to first see nature and identify that nature was the thing in the image that they wanted to focus their attention on in images of urban environments; the results support hypotheses 2 and 3 .

Not all outcomes of Study 3 replicated Study 2 results. One of the biggest differences between the two studies was in the correlations with affect. For the first attention task, not only were there differences in the significance, but there was also a difference in the direction of the correlations. In Study 3, those who reported noticing the nature first in the image also reported more positive affect and less negative affect in the last four weeks. In Study 2, however, the associations were in opposite directions (negative for positive affect and positive for negative affect) and also non-significant. Similar discrepancies were found with the direction for the voluntary attention item, but the correlations were consistently non-significant in both studies. It is unclear why we are seeing these dispersions of the correlations. One explanation may be due to sampling error. To explore this, scatterplots of the correlations and Mahalanobis distance values were computed. For the significant correlations between affect and first attention in Study 3, outliers were identified. Without the outliers included, the association was reduced to nonsignificant, but stayed in the same direction as the original result. Thus, this suggests that the small correlations were sensitive to outliers 8 . The difference in the pattern may be due to Study ), but also relatively small. The correlations between the behavioural tasks and affect are fragile and may need more investigation for explanation with more comprehensive findings than can be provided in the current studies.

Differently from positive and negative affect, the direction of the association between awe and the first attention task was consistently positive, but differed in significance across the two. Only in Study 3 were participants who reported noticing nature first in the image also reporting feeling more awe in the last four weeks. Additionally, the correlation between first attention and awe in Study 2 was less consistent across the different sets, suggesting that the small correlation was fragile. In contrast, awe was not associated with voluntary attention in either study. These relationships were not dependent on outliers.

There were also mixed results in the replication of the face-valid items and measures correlating with the attention items. Consistently across both attention items in Study 2 and 3, those who paid more attention to nature also reported doing more noticing nature activities.

However, the two NRS items "Even in the city, I notice the nature around me" and "I take notice of wildlife wherever I am ") were not significantly with the first attention item in Study 2, but they were for Study 3. Across both studies, the NRS items were significantly associated with voluntary attention item.

Overall, across two studies, the attention behavioural tasks for noticing nature were associated with nature relatedness. With a consistent correlation in two samples, I am more confident in this association.

div.head: General Discussion
div.p: The overall goal of this dissertation was to explore if nature related people were more likely to notice nature in everyday moments in an urban environment. To control the amount of nature participants were exposed to, everyday nature was operationalized by showing participants images of urban environments with some degree of nature on a computer screen.

Noticing nature was examined through two processes: perception (Phase 1) and attention (Phase 2). Perception was defined as a person's interpretation of nature (i.e., if a person does not recognize the nature, they will not notice it). Attention was defined in two ways: 1) if immediate attention was drawn towards nature and 2) if their preferred attention was oriented towards it. I hypothesized that nature related individuals would perceive more and pay more attention to nature in images of urban environments on a computer. Across both phases, mixed results were observed. In Phase 1, differing from the hypothesis, there was no relationship between participants' ratings of nature perception (either through the 7-point scale item or the percentage item) and their levels of nature relatedness. In contrast, hypotheses 2 and 3 were supported and replicated in Phase 2; nature related people were more likely to have their attention drawn toward the nature in images of urban environments and were also more likely to choose to focus their attention on it. Together, the results suggest a promising step in understanding nature related individuals' affinity for nature in their everyday life.

div.head: Noticing Nature Tasks: What did I measure, and what does it mean?
div.p: I created four tasks related to the two processes to assess the hypothesized correlation between noticing nature and nature relatedness. The perception process was measured through two rating scales that asked how much nature was in an image: 1) the 7-point rating scale; 2) a percentage rating item. The attention process was measured through two image-based click assessments: 1) clicking on the first thing they noticed in the image (first attention); 2) clicking on the thing they wanted to focus their attention on in the image (voluntary attention). Though the results of the studies suggested two of the four noticing nature tasks (i.e., the attention noticing nature tasks) were associated with nature relatedness, it was essential to also calibrate how much noticing nature I could capture with my tasks.

There was a lack of support for the idea that nature related individuals noticed more nature through the two perception tasks. It is unclear whether the absence of an association with nature relatedness is due to no true relationship or rather that the measurement tool inaccurately assessed the concept of perception (or noticing nature in general) I intended to measure. The psychometric results corroborate that there is enough variability in the task to examine individual differences (identified through psychometric analyses and multilevel models). Still, the lack of association with face-valid self-report noticing nature measure (NNA; Richardson et al., 2021) and items (two individual NRS items; Nisbet et al., 2009) suggests that the tasks measured something outside of noticing nature. There was also a lack of predictive validity for the other variables (i.e., nature relatedness, affect 10 , and frequency of noticing nature activities). Thus, the confidence in the perception tasks as behavioural measures of noticing nature is low.

In contrast, there was more support suggesting that the attention tasks were better measures of noticing nature than the perception tasks. Both attention items showed predictive validity in their association with nature relatedness. The two nature attention tasks were also related to the face-valid measure (NNA) and items (two items from the NRS) of noticing nature, supporting that the tasks were behavioural measures of noticing nature. More specifically, 10 There was a single correlation between the 7-point scale rating item of perception and positive affect. This correlation is relatively small in size (.17) with a large confidence interval (.04 to .28). This suggests that the correlation may be due to sampling variation (i.e., chance). Thus, the confidence in the correlation is not high.

participants who indicated that they noticed nature first and voluntarily wanted to focus on it in the images also self-reported doing more noticing nature activities. Together, this gives me more confidence in the attention tasks as a better tool for measuring noticing nature and, thus, provide evidence that nature related people notice more nature in urban environments through the process of attention. Henceforth, the discussion will center mostly around the attention-based noticing nature behavioural tasks.

div.head: Attention and Perception
div.p: The definitions of the processes of perception and attention explored in the dissertation were more colloquial in nature. In cognitive psychology, perception is defined as the conscious experience that comes from sensory information and attention is defined as focusing on an object, place, thought, or activity (Goldstein, 2011). In the current studies, I defined perception as the interpretation of nature; attention as awareness being drawn and focused towards nature.
Even though the colloquial definitions were an outside of cognitive psychology, the exploration of the "processes" are still related to the field, in general.

For example, the two "processes" of attention measured in the current studies are both considered to be explicit processing of attention (i.e., involves conscious processing) because of the way I measured them. I measured the two attentions by having participants click on the image. Thus, even if the first attention task may seem like it is measuring implicit/automatic/exogenous attention, because the participants were still consciously able to identify what they did notice first and actively clicked on the image, it is an explicit reporting of first attention. This is different than eye tracking techniques that measure fixation points (i.e., measuring where in the image the eye is pausing to focus on) of a scene. In Bingjing et al. (2022) study, the eye tracking measured fixation on the natural and urban elements of the 360° scene. In this study (Bingjing et al., 2022), it was not clear that participants were aware that they were spending more time fixating on areas, such as nature related people fixated more on the natural elements of the scene.

The more explicit reporting of attention used in the dissertation may be biased by the implicit selective attention that is occurring subconsciously. As research in cognitive psychology would suggest, when perceiving or paying attention to anything there is a step of prioritization that occurs to bring information from the senses to the subjective mind; this prioritization can come from both bottom-up and top-down processing (van Ede & Nobre, 2023). Thus, my participants have gone through this prioritization subconsciously before being aware of the object there are noticing to respond to my questions. With my current results, I can not necessarily say that participants high in nature relatedness prioritize nature in a scene with multiple stimuli, but Bingjing and colleagues (2022) would suggest that they are fixating more on natural elements and my studies would support they are aware enough to explicit report the nature. Nevertheless, there may be another level of awareness that may not be occurring. For example, it is not clear if the people who click nature the most across the images would also selfreport that they were noticing nature more often than not. In other words, they may not be aware that across all 50 clicks on the behavioural task their attention was being drawn towards the natural elements rather than the urban elements.

div.head: Implicit and Explicit Noticing Nature
div.p: Nature relatedness is an individual difference characteristic that would fit within an individual's self-concept (i.e., the description of who a person thinks they are). The self-concept can influence a person's attitudes and behaviours, where they have thoughts or do activities that fit their self-concept. Not only has previous research shown that some attitudes and behaviours concept of nature relatedness, as implied. Additionally, the links of the two NRS items related to noticing nature with the explicit behavioural tasks reinforce that these two items of the NRS accurately assess psychological processes or self-reported behaviour of noticing nature. For instance, people who report they are likely to notice the nature around them, even in a city (i.e., item 8 of the NRS), were more likely to do so in an urban image task.

Even though there is an association between the implicit (the task) and the explicit noticing nature (the self-report measure and items), there are differences between the methods that are important to consider. The explicit measures are general assessments of attitudes and behaviours towards noticing nature, whereas the built tasks are momentary assessments. Thus, it is not clear how much the current tasks are momentary and unstable or if the act of noticing more nature measured with the tasks may be more trait-like, where the responses would be more stable. The replicated association between nature relatedness and the attention tasks would suggest that the task responses are more stable like an individual's self-concept. However, the small correlations indicate that other factors may associate with responses. Without clear testretest assessments, the consistency in the tasks is not clear. The task would benefit from future research employing multiple administrations.

div.head: Nature Relatedness, Noticing Nature, and Affect
div.p: The notion that nature related individuals are more likely to notice nature in their daily lives stems from the proposition that noticing nature may lead to increased happiness. Thus, exploring the associations between nature relatedness, noticing nature, and affect in the dissertation studies extends the research on the connection between nature relatedness and happiness (Capaldi et al., 2014;Pritchard et al., 2020). There may be a few reasons why nature related individuals are generally happier. One of these reasons may be that they are spending more time in nature, which has been previously shown (Colleony et al., 2017;Desrochers et al., 2022;Flowers et al., 2016;Lin et al., 2014;Nisbet et al., 2009;Shannahan et al., 2015b;Soga & Akasaka, 2019), but it may also be that they tend to notice nature in everyday moments. For example, are nature-related individuals better able to notice small parts of nature (microexposure to nature) in their everyday life to make them happy? No previous research has directly examined this, but there is suggestive support.

In the dissertation studies, I found mixed results for this notion. Overall, in the current studies, nature related people were happier (measured through positive affect; correlations ranged from .13 to .18 in the three studies, see Appendix F for more details). There was also an indication that nature related individuals do notice more nature when assessing it through the self-report measure of how often they engage in noticing nature activities (i.e., the NNA measure by Richardson et al., 2021;correlations ranged from .60 to .65, see Appendix F for more details) and the attention behavioural task of noticing nature 11 . However, it is not clear that noticing nature is associated with affect (i.e., there were mixed findings regarding the self-report and behavioural noticing nature measures being associated with positive affect). Thus, the links between noticing nature and positive affect are too inconsistent to see clear support.

Even though the current findings give mixed evidence for noticing nature being a reason nature related people are happier, it is still plausible that the association exists. The behavioural tasks were created to assess if participants notice more nature in their everyday life by simulating real-life views through images and were not necessarily meant to increase one's mood, as is often done in nature research. With this said, being able to assess participants' ability to notice 11 Nature related individuals were not more likely to notice nature through the perception behavioural tasks. However, as previously discussed, it may be that the perception task was not an appropriate measure of noticing nature.

nature does not mean that they have noticed more nature recently, which could account for their mood scores over the last four weeks. As research shows, people spend a large majority of their time indoors (Matz et al., 2015), and if they spend time outdoors, their neighbourhoods, in general, tend to have minimal biodiversity (Turner et al., 2004); thus, even though nature related people may pay attention to nature, they may not have had the opportunity to do so. The fact that participants who reported doing more noticing nature activities reported that they had more positive moods over the last four weeks would help support the idea that noticing nature improved positive mood (correlations ranged from .14 to .32, see Appendix F for more details).

The broader body of literature also provides support for the subject. The three studies by Passmore and colleagues (Passmore & Holder, 2016;Passmore et al., 2022ab) provide supportive evidence that performing a noticing nature activity over the course of two weeks improves well-being (i.e., there was a change in well-being outcomes post-intervention from the baseline values); further, noticing nature improved well-being regardless of time spent in nature.

Additionally, when exploring if noticing nature may be a reason that nature related individuals are happier, there is some conceptual support in this study and others, but it may be harder to see statistically in research. For instance, many things make up why a person may be happier, such as personality traits (e.g., extraversion, emotional stability; Diener et al., 1999), social relationships (Diener & Seligman, 2002), and even genes (Lykken & Tellegen, 1996;Nes et al., 2006). Plus, there may be other more specific predictors of happiness that a nature related person would do that make them happy, such as spending more time in nature, doing more proenvironmental behaviours, more physical activity, and reduced screen time, which have all have previously been associated with increased feelings of positive affect (Buecker et al., 2021;McKay & Schmitt, 2019;McMahan & Estes, 2015;Molina-Cando et al., 2021;Pedersen et al., 2022;Zawadzki et al., 2020). Thus, noticing nature may be trying to explain a small amount of variance in a substantial context and may get lost or overshadowed by other predictors. However, the little support for noticing nature is still important to understand as it may help, if even small, improve people's happiness.

So, even though I did not find a clear link between noticing nature and positive affect, it may be that noticing nature is only a small part of the path to happiness (see Figure 19). There may be other steps of engaging or augmenting experiences with nature that help see the benefit from it. As Gaston & Soga (2020) put it, interactions and experiences with nature are different;

an interaction is a more superficial contact with nature through the senses, such as smell, sight, and sound (this could be considered more similar to my definition of noticing nature), whereas an experience is more of an engagement with nature. An example of an experience with nature may be savouring, characterized as actively doing something to enhance and prolong pleasurable feelings. Research has shown that savouring nature exposures can benefit well-being (Sato et al., 2017). Savouring activities, such as being present to absorb the moment, focusing on the moment to intensify it, taking a moment to feel grateful for the moment, and doing something to be able to share the moment with others (e.g., take an image of the natural element), could all be considered the next step of augmenting or enhancing nature experience after noticing it. In other words, a person first notices (or interacts with) nature and then may do something to augment the moments to turn it into an experience with nature. Thus, it may be that nature related individuals in an everyday moment notice the little bits of nature around them and then take a second to engage with it (e.g., potentially savour the moment with nature). To the best of my knowledge, no research has examined whether nature related individuals are better at savouring nature moments. One study found that high nature relatedness individuals identified that they valued nature (had appreciation towards it) over the pandemic (Desrochers et al., 2022). Also, in Lomas's (2019) lexical enquiry of untranslatable words across the world that discuss one's ecoconnection, appreciation and savouring were identified as relevant themes, where the act of paying attention and appreciating the nuances of nature was a way to connect with it. Together these findings, in combination with nature related people wanting to pay attention to nature (i.e., results for the current dissertation) and reporting doing more noticing nature activities (which may be more similar to augmenting noticing nature to an experience), suggest that nature related people may not only notice more nature, but also take the next step towards savouring the microexposure. This path (Figure 19) of interactions with nature to experiences with nature may improve state nature connection and subjective well-being. Having said that, it may also suggest that those low on nature relatedness may be missing out on the opportunity to savour nature because it is impossible to savour nature without noticing it (which they do less). of sensory inputs, including smells, sounds, tastes, textures, and many sights. The images used in the studies were limited to only displaying particular sights without any other sensory inputs to the participants. This may reduce the generalizability of the effect outside of a laboratory setting.

It is unclear if nature related people would still be able to pay attention to nature amidst a multitude of competing information. Yet, the use of real nature exposure may prove difficult to control. I believe that noticing nature and the amount of nature exposure overlap, such that the more nature that one is exposed to will directly increase one's ability to notice it. Thus, it may be difficult to control the amount of nature each participant is being exposed to in real urban environments with some degree of nature. However, more creative ways of exploring noticing nature in real natural spaces should be explored next.

Further, the link of noticing nature with nature relatedness may rely on the specific images used for the tasks. The images used were of urban environments with varying degrees of nature. The natural elements in the images used were trees, plants (planted in pots or on the ground), bodies of water, green roof, mountains, and some wildlife (birds, ducks, wolves, dogs, and horses). These are only a few examples of what could be considered nature in an urban environment. As biologist Hanna Bjørgaas (2023) wants us to discover, many species live and thrive in urban spaces that we may not have noticed before, but are as fascinating as complex nature in pristine landscapes. Therefore, further considerations should be taken to broaden the scope of natural elements found in urban environments.

In a similar light, these natural elements found in the included images were natural elements that fit my definition of nature 12 . Due to the lack of a clear definition of nature across people (Hartig & Kahn, 2016), I was faced with the decision of creating a priori boxes on Qualtrics of the natural elements in Phase 2. I chose to select the prototypical natural elements to include in the a priori boxes (i.e., the natural elements mentioned above). In these decisions, I did not consider the sky and clouds as natural elements for the images in the studies, but they could be defined as features of nature (Fehnker et al., 2021;Shaw, 2018). Additionally, when creating the a priori boxes, it was sometimes difficult to distinguish between the urban and natural areas in the images because natural elements often have irregular shapes. I did my best only to include the natural elements in the boxes (not the urban elements) and ensure I included all aspects of the natural element; however, it was not easily done. Some boxes may have a bit of overlap with other things in the image. This may create errors in the coded responses. All a priori boxes can be seen in the supplement on OSF.

There might also be cultural definitions of what counts as nature, which may impact the tool's generalizability or usefulness in cultures or geographical locations different than North America. In both studies of Phase 2, there was considerable consistency in the results, but these samples were of students and community members currently living in North America. The images used were meant to include typical natural elements found in North American cities.

Previous research has shown that even the definition of nature is different around the world. Coscieme et al. (2019) found that in Western society, nature generally means pristine without humans, whereas in other languages (and cultures), nature may be defined by the integral connection between nature and humans (e.g., in many indigenous languages) or defined by its spiritual context. As language is important for how people see and understand the world, the different definitions of the word nature may impose different conceptualizations of nature.

Additionally, as much as there are differences between different areas of North America, there are also differences in the natural elements found around the world. For example, China is home to more flowing plant species than North and South America combined (Boudreau et al., 2023), and holds 10% of the world's flowering plant species (van Hoose, 2018). Thus, there may be native flower plant species that are expected in China (even in its city limits) that are not anticipated in other geographical areas. Together, this suggests that if the current tasks (or even the association of the tasks and nature relatedness) were explored in other cultural and geographical locations, further considerations should be taken regarding the natural elements of the images.

One of the goals of the dissertation was to explore the validity of the behavioural measure of noticing nature. I did this by exploring psychometric analyses; however, the behavioural measures of noticing nature I created may be further refined. For one, there was a lack of support for the first hypothesis stating that nature related individuals were more likely to perceive nature in an urban environment. As discussed, even though the measure of perception measured something reliably, it is not clear that this was the concept of noticing nature. Future research may attempt to explore a new tool for measuring noticing nature through perception. For instance, perception may be best examined through the limits of perception or the perceptual threshold by making the research question more implicit. This could be done by examining short-timed windows of exposure and asking participants to identify whether there was nature.

For the behavioural task of attention, there was support that the measure reliably measured noticing nature. However, further refinement steps could be taken, such as test-retest stability, to explore if the measure is more like a stable trait. Attention could also be explored in more diverse images than the ones used in the current dissertation. For example, would those low in nature relatedness be more likely to pay attention to the urban objects of a primarily natural setting? Further, to extend the current support that nature related individuals were more likely to pay attention to nature, future research should also explore how the attention behavioural measure of noticing nature may be associated with other variables. One potentially related variable is pro-environmental behaviour. Previously, nature connection (relatedness) was associated with pro-environmental behaviours through both correlational and experimental explorations (McKay & Schmitt, 2019). Also, nature exposure is associated with proenvironmental behaviour (see review by DeVille et al., 2021). However, research has yet to examine how noticing nature may be associated with pro-environmental behaviour. In extra analyses not explored in the publication (Desrochers et al., 2022), my colleagues and I found associations between the single items, "I notice and see wildlife more," and "I value nature more (appreciation)," with doing more for the environment during the pandemic (Fall 2020) than before, r(554) = .26 p < .001 and r(554) = .24 p < .001. This may suggest that people who notice nature (and appreciate it) may be more likely to have pro-environmental attitudes and do something helpful for the environment. In the current studies, no pro-environmental attitudes or behaviour measures were included. However, the perspective subscale of the NRS is associated with topics of pro-environmental attitudes, making it the most similar measure in the dataset. The voluntary attention behavioural task was associated with the NRS perspective, suggesting that those who chose to pay attention to nature in urban environment images may also treat the environment better. Further, those who reported doing more noticing nature activities also had higher scores on the NRS perspective subscale (correlations ranged from .31 to .36, see Appendix F for more details). While these cross-sectional results do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship, it serves as an initial step in investigating how noticing nature may help promote sustainable behaviours. However, further exploration should be taken with better measures of pro-environmental attitudes and behaviour.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In light of the ongoing conversation about the adverse effects of the extinction of experience, it is crucial to examine how individuals in urban areas can still engage with, connect with, and benefit from the natural world. As Shannahan et al. (2015a) suggest, two ways to combat extinction of experience is through: 1) increasing the amount of nature in urban environments and 2) assisting people in discovering how to connect with the nature readily available to them. Increasing the amount of nature in urban environments may be effective in promoting nature exposure, but it is also costly, and it is generally undervalued and underimplemented by cities' decisions makers. Showing people how to notice or connect with the nature they already have access to is a cost-effective, individual action, and an easy way to increase nature benefits in people. It shows people the "magic of the mundane" (Dobson et al., 2021). It may also, in turn, pressure policymakers to improve nearby nature to allow for better opportunities to notice (and maybe even savour) nature. Nisbet and Zelenski (2011) showed that people underestimated how a walk in nature would improve their mood, while overestimating their predicted mood for an urban walk. This may show that people are less likely to assume that exposing themselves to nature will benefit them, which will most likely reduce their likelihood of exposing themselves to nature. The first two sections were the blocked nature attention tasks. There were two different types of nature attention tasks to explore the two distinct versions of attention being paid to nature in urban images. The different attention questions were presented to participants in blocks, similar to Phase 1 Study 1. Participants were shown the set of images and asked a single attention question. Then, they were shown the images again and asked the other question. Participants were exposed to the same set of images for both blocks, randomly ordered. Because the two different attention questions can affect each other (i.e. ordering effect), the different questions were presented to participants in a set order. In Block A, participants were asked about the first thing they noticed in the image. This is known as first attention. In Block B, the participants were asked to choose an object/thing in the image that they wanted to focus their attention on. This is known as voluntary attention. After completing the two blocks, participants filled out the demographic questionnaire, the 21-item Nature Relatedness scale (NRS;Nisbet et al., 2009; ∝ = .79), Noticing Nature Activities Survey (NNA; Richardson et al., 2021; ∝ = .88), and the Scale of Positive and Negative Experiences (SPANE; Diener et al., 2010; PA ∝ = .88 NA ∝ = .80 Awe ∝ = .83). Finally, participants answered demographic questions, such as age, gender, ethnicity, where they grew up, where they were currently living, and what type of device they used to fill out the questionnaire.
