div.head: Methods
div.p: Participants. Much like Phase 1, running a proper a priori power analysis to justify the sample size is challenging due to the lack of previous work done in this area. However, a sample of 300 participants was identified as appropriate to recruit. This aligns with a simulation suggesting that correlations stabilize at a sample of 250 participants with 80% confidence (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013). With a sample of 250 participants, alpha set at .05, and power set at 90%, an effect size of .12, in either direction, can be identified (as highlighted by a sensitivity power analysis run in G*Power).

Optional stopping techniques were used to stop the recruitment of participants at 100 to check the variability of the two attention items for each image. This strengthened the tools used to examine the association between nature attention and nature relatedness. This phase had more difficulty in finding images with an appropriate amount of variability in the items. div.head: Discussion
div.p: In this phase of the dissertation, I explored if nature related individuals would notice more nature through the process of attention. Participants were asked to click on the first thing they noticed in the image (first attention) and what in the image they would want to focus their attention on (voluntary attention) for 50 images of urban environments with varying degrees of nature. Given the tool-building nature of the investigation, psychometric analyses were conducted to examine the extent of variability among the images. This step was deemed more difficult to accomplish than for Study 1. Three optional stopping rounds were conducted with 100 participants each before finding 50 images that demonstrated enough variability through descriptive statistics, a standardized distribution of the images, reliability analyses (Cronbach's alpha, Omega, and split-half reliability), and inter-image correlations. This variability was also considered acceptable with the full sample of 294 participants. Additionally, unconditional logistic multilevel models identified that there was enough between-people variability in both attention items to explore the association with nature relatedness. The overall results showed a positive association between both attention items and nature relatedness; these relationships were robust across the different sets of images. This suggests that, with my current tools, participants higher in nature relatedness were more likely to notice nature first and also choose to focus their attention on it in an urban environment. Therefore, the results did support H2 and H3.

Be that as it may, a single study showing small associations between noticing nature through attention and nature relatedness may stem from a sampling error. The correlations of both first attention and voluntary attention with nature relatedness are less than modest in size.

These correlations may be due to the sample of students and may not be generalizable to a larger population. Even though an appropriate sample size allowed for the detection of a small Procedure. These items include, but are not limited to, attitudes towards sustainability (e.g. "I always think about how my actions affect the environment."), experiences with or exposure to nature ("I don't often go out in nature"reverse-coded), and also noticing nature ("I take notice of wildlife wherever I am" and "Even in the middle of the city, I notice nature around me"). These items that assess nature relatedness highlight the attitudes and behaviours that are a part of the self-concept of highly nature related people. Thus, noticing nature is implied to be a fundamental aspect of their self-concepts, even though research has not behaviourally demonstrated this.

For the purpose of the dissertation, I created new behavioural tasks of noticing nature to be able to test if nature related individuals do, in fact, notice more nature (implicit behaviour) rather than relying on the already-created self-report measure (NNA; Richardson et al., 2021) or the responses to the two individual items of the NRS related to noticing nature. There are methodological limitations to using self-report measures. For example, the measure of nature relatedness (NRS; Nisbet et al., 2009) relies on participants to self-reflect, recall attitudes and behaviours, and then respond honestly to questions to identify their level of nature relatedness. A

participant may report noticing nature because it aligns with their self-concept (i.e., "this is something I would do") rather than recalling actual behaviours (i.e., the discrepancy between the self and behaviours). Therefore, examining behavioural measures of key concepts that align with or help characterize nature relatedness is important.

div.head: Negative Affect
div.p: Negative affect was also measured in the three studies. Across all associations (i.e., nature relatedness, self-report and behavioural noticing nature) with negative affect, there was less consistency than for positive affect. For one, nature relatedness only showed significantly lower levels of negative affect in Study 3 (r[1053] = -.13 p < 001, see Appendix F for more details). Neither of the meta-analyses (Capaldi et al., 2014;Pritchard et al., 2020) previously examined the association between nature connectedness and negative affect; thus, it is less clear whether this result is unusual. However, it does seem to be in line with the previous finding in Nisbet et al. (2009), where nature relatedness was not significantly associated with negative affect in three studies. The lack of consistent negative affect associations is similar to McMahan and Estes's (2015) meta-analytic results showing that the benefits of nature exposure were stronger and more stable for positive affect than for negative affect. Exposure to nature is different from nature relatedness, but nature related individuals tend to spend more time in nature and (as suggested in this dissertation) notice more nature. This may imply that the association between nature relatedness and negative affect may also be less consistent.

div.head: Limitations and Future Directions
div.p: While the current studies of the dissertation have contributed valuable insights to the literature on how nature related individuals notice nature, it is essential to acknowledge that the current studies are not without limitations. For one, I used virtual nature, through images, in the current dissertation to control the amount of nature the participants were being exposed to. The use of virtual nature also made it easier to run the studies with both students and members of the larger community (i.e., MTurk workers from Canada and the United States). However, images do not capture the full essence of everyday moments. At all times, a person experiences a variety

The current dissertation showed preliminary support for the idea that nature related individuals may be better equipped to pay attention to small fragments of nature in urban environments that they already have available to them. They are also more likely to report doing noticing nature activities, like watching wildlife, listening to birdsongs, and smelling the wildflowers. Even though there were inconsistent findings on the behavioural noticing nature tasks associated with well-being in the current studies, the link between self-report noticing nature and well-being, in combination with the broader literature, proposes that noticing nature may still be the first step (process) on the path to happiness.

div.head: Appendix C Principle Component Analysis Results for Study 1 The 7-point Rating Scale Item
div.p: As an exploratory psychometric analysis for the full sample, I ran principle components analyses (PCA) to measure the underlying explanatory variables through different independent linear combinations (APA, 2015). Field (2013) outlines in the textbook Discovering Statistics Using IBSM SPSS Statistics the general procedure for PCA as followed: 1) check for appropriate sample size, 2) check correlations between variables (in our case images), 3) factor extraction, 4) factor rotation (however, because I only expect to have a single solution, rotation will be unnecessary) , and then 5) reliability. I will follow these procedure suggestions for both items.

For the 7-point scale rating item, the sample size was deemed appropriate for PCA through Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy (KMO), KMO = .93. Additionally, when examining the KMO for each individual image, all 50 images had a KMO of .80 or above, indicating an appropriate sample size for PCA. When examining inter-image correlations, Barlett's test was significant, 𝑋 2 (𝑑𝑓 = 1225) = 7400.13 p < .001, indicating that our interimage correlation matrix is significantly different than an identity matrix. Field (2013) suggests that inter-item correlations should be significant, above the value of .3 to show that the images should are measuring the same thing, and below .8 to reduce multicollinearity. None of the images showed strong correlations (above .8). However, on the low end, every image had at least 11 correlations below .3. With this in mind, significance was examined instead. Twenty-two images had all significant inter-image correlations (this set was labelled best images). Twentytwo images of the 28 images that had non-significant inter-image correlations had less than 6 inter-image correlations that were non-significant (this set was labelled satisfactory), whereas the set labelled problematic were images with the range of 5 to 14 non-significant correlations ( 6The Percentage Rating Item Next, I ran a PCA for the percentage rating item. The overall KMO suggests an appropriate sample size for PCA, KMO = .94, and the KMO value was above the threshold of .80 for all individual images. When examining the inter-image correlations, the Barlett's test was significant, 𝑋 2 (𝑑𝑓 = 1225) = 6793.21 p < .001, indicating this matrix is significantly different from an identity matrix. When looking at non-significant inter-image correlations, there were only two images that had above five non-significant correlations. Image 10 had eight nonsignificant correlations, whereas Image 23 had five. These two images were removed from the set. None of the correlations were too high (above .8). Every image had at minimum 3 interimage correlations that were below the threshold of . All items loaded the strongest on the single factor. Therefore, no other images were identified to be removed.

The reliability for the percentage rating item, with 48 images identified as appropriate, was good: Cronbach's ∝ = .96, Omega = .96 95% CI [.95, .97], split-half reliability r(279) = .92 p < .001 95% CI [.89, .95]. The values of reliability through Cronbach's alpha and Omega are the same as when using the sample of 50 images; however, the split-half reliability was slightly better for this set.

div.head: Appendix E Psychometric Analysis Results for Optional Stopping Steps of Study 2
div.p: Similar to Phase 1, optional stopping was used to examine the variability of the attention items for each item. This was done at a sample of 100 participants before recruiting the full sample target of 300 participants. After recruiting 100 participants, the variability of each attention item was explored separately. As pre-registered (see OSF), if more than seven images were identified as having poor variability, they were removed, replaced, and recruitment began again at zero. For Study 2, three unique optional stopping psychometric analyses were run before identifying appropriate images to continue to recruiting the full sample target of 300. The results of the three rounds are described below.

div.head: Round 1
div.p: The variability of the two attention items were explored separately. To test variability of the images for both items, descriptive statistics (minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, and frequency of the are clicked), standardized distribution (Z-scores and visual representation), reliability analysis and inter-image correlations were explored.

div.head: First Attention
div.p: The first attention mean across all images was 0.18 (SD = 0.19; Min = 0.00, Max = 0.81).
This suggesting, across all clicks, nature was clicked for the first attention item 18% of the time.

The amount of nature area clicks varied per image, ranging from 0% to 81%. All quantitative results can be seen in Table E-1. When exploring the variability in the first attention clicks on either the nature area or the other areas, three images were identified to have no variance in the responses (i.e. all participants chose the other area instead of the nature area of the image). This warrants the removal of explored how the standardized distribution with z-transformed means looked when removing images with varying degrees of percentage of nature clicks. I did this by examine four different set of images: 1) images with no variance removed; 2) images with 5% or less of the clicks for first attention as on the nature area removed; 3) images with the nature area been chosen 10% or less were removed; 4) images with 15% or less was removed. See Table E-

div.head: Voluntary Attention
div.p: Overall, the mean of the voluntary attention item across all images was 0.25 (SD = 0.19); therefore, nature was clicked for the first attention item, on average, 25% of the time. This did differ per image, with a range of 0% to 75%. All quantitative information about the voluntary attention for each image van be seen in Table E-3 Compared to the first attention item, only two images had no variance. Images 34 and 40 did not have anyone choose the nature as the area on which they wanted to focus their attention.
Therefore, these images were identified as poor images and were removed.

The reliability was good across the 48 items (Images 34 and 40 removed), Cronbach's ∝ = .82. There were 34 items that were identified as good by showing that the alpha decreases if the item is removed, whereas 14 items were identified as bad by showing that the alpha would decrease if removed. However, the decrease was very minimal (the maximum increase was by .007). Therefore, this criterion will not be used to highlight images to removal.

div.head: Looking Across Both Items
div.p: Now that images were highlighted as poor for either for the first attention item or the voluntary attention item, to make a decision about what images will be replaced before restarting the recruitment, I have also examined how images performed across both items. In the psychometric analysis for the first attention item, it was shown that the distribution becomes more normal when using only images with more than 15% nature clicks. For voluntary attention, when removing images with up to less than 20% nature clicks, the distribution does not significantly change. With this in mind, I have chosen to select images to keep depending on at least 15% nature clicks across both (i.e. the image must have performed with at least 15% for each item). With this criteria, 18 images had a good percentage of nature clicks and therefore, would be kept. These images were : 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 12, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 30, 35, 41, 42, 43, 46, and 47. The 32 images identified a poor were replaced.

div.head: Round 2
div.p: After the replacement of the 32 images, a new set of 100 participants were recruited to explore the variability of the new set of images (18 old images and 32 new images).

div.head: First Attention
div.p: On average, across all the clicks, the nature areas were clicked 26% of the time (M = 0.26, SD = 0.18; Min = 0.00, Max = 0.81). This is a larger mean than Round 1 (M = 0.18, SD. =

.19), even though the minimum and maximum are the same. All 49 images with variance showed both positive and negative correlations with each other. The inter-image correlations ranged from -0.41 to 0.61. All quantitative results of the psychometric analyses for all 50 images can be seen in Table E-5.

When exploring the variability of all 50 items, one image (Image 61) was identified as having no variance and therefore was removed from the analysis. The overall Cronbach's alpha of these 49 images was again quite low at .67, but this was larger than Round 1 (Cronbach's 𝛼 = .61). The reliability was quite robust to the removal of a single image, where the alpha was reduced by a maximum of .02 or increased by a maximum of . 03. In this robustness test, 10 images were highlighted as poor images (i.e. where the Cronbach's alpha was increased if the image was removed), 38 images were good images (i.e. where the Cronbach's alpha was decreased if removed), and a single image showed no change in Cronbach's alpha if removed.
Due to the small amount of change in Cronbach's alpha, this criteria was dropped for identifying images to be replaced.

div.head: Voluntary Attention
div.p: The mean across all 50 images was 0.33 (SD = 0.20; Min = .05, Max = 0.80), indicating that, on average, the nature area was clicked 33% of the time. This is higher than the 25% from Round 1. This varied per image with a minimum percentage of 5% and a maximum of 80%. All quantitative results can be seen in Table E-7.

The reliability of all images (i.e. no images were identified as having no variance) was ∝ = .87, which was .05 points above the reliability of Round 1. When exploring the robustness of the reliability, the majority of images were identified as good images with 41 images showing the Cronbach's alpha was reduced when the image was removed (i.e. identified as good images for aggregation) and 6 images where the removal had no effect on the alpha value. For the three poor images, the removal of the image showed a maximum improvement of the Cronbach's ∝ by .003, which is very minimal. Thus, this was not used a criteria for identifying images to be replaced.

The standardized distribution for the 50 images was not normal visually (see Figure E-8) nor quantitatively, Shapiro-Wilkes estimate = .93 p = .004. Similar to previous psychometric analyses, robustness tests were run to examine if the standardized distribution would become normal when removing images on the lower end of the distribution (i.e. images with the smallest percentage of nature chosen as the area participants wanted to focus their attention on). The quantitative results of these robustness tests can be seen in Table E-8. When running the robustness removing images with 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% or less nature, the distribution did not become normal visually or statistically (see Table E-8; Shapiro-Wilkes p > .05). None of means were above or below 3 SD, indicating that there were no outliers identified. Thus, no images were highlighted to be removed to improve normality of the distribution.

div.head: Looking at both
div.p: Similar to round 1, I have decided to make decisions about the images by examining how they performed across both items. To make the decision on the criteria, I will look towards my robustness tests. For the first attention item, the standardized distribution becomes more normal when removing images with 10% or less nature clicks. For voluntary attention, when removing images with 20% or less, there was no changes to the normality of the distribution. Therefore, I have chosen to select keeping images which have above 10% nature clicks across both images. If I use this criterion, I would be removing 16 images (51,53,56,59,61,65,66,68,69,70,72,74,76,78,79,80). However, when exploring how these 16 images performed for each item, there are a few items that underperformed for first attention item, but did well on the voluntary attention item. There are five images that fit this description. These images were retained. This reduces my number of images to replace to 11. These images were: 51, 56, 61, 65, 66, 68, 69, 72, 76, 78, and 80. These 11 images were replaced.

div.head: Round 3
div.p: After replacing the 11 images, a new sample of 100 participants were recruited to explore the variability of the new set of images (i.e. 11 new ones and 39 old ones).

div.head: First Attention
div.p: The mean value for the first attention across all images was 0.31 (SD = 0.22; Min.= 0.00, Max = 0.95), indicating that, across all the clicks made by participants, participants clicked the nature area approximately 31% of the time. This mean is the largest between the three rounds.

This percentage did vary across the images (Min = 0%, Max = 95%). All quantitative results can be seen in or below 3 SD, indicating that there were no outliers identified. Thus, no images were identified to be removed to improve normality of the distribution.

div.head: Looking at both
div.p: Across both items, there was only a single image that had no variance. Image 70 showed no variance in the first attention item. In the previous round, this image had a small percentage of nature clicks (3% in Round 2). For voluntary attention item, this is the image with the least amount of nature clicks, with 12%.

In contrast with the other rounds, the robustness tests for normality were unchanged across all tests. This suggested that there was not an appropriate cut off point to identify images for removal. With this in mind, I have decided to move on with recruitment of the full sample (N = 300) with the current set of images (i.e. all images are retained).

div.head: Extra Analyses
div.p: To examine if the means across the three rounds of psychometric analyses are in fact different, a one-way ANOVA was run with each item's mean as the dependent variable and the psychometric rounds was the independent variable. For both attention items, there was a significant difference in means across Rounds (first attention: F(2, 149) = 7.84 p = .008 𝜂 2 = 0.6; voluntary attention: F(2, 149) = 7.84 p < .001 𝜂 2 = 0.10. The only significant Scheffe post-hoc comparison for both items was between Rounds 1 and 3, where the mean of Round 3 was significantly larger than the mean of Round 1 (item 1: 𝑀 𝑑𝑖𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑟𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒(3-1) = 0.12 p = .008; item 2:
𝑀 𝑑𝑖𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑟𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒(3-1) = 0.16 p < .001).
I also explored the correlation between the first attention and voluntary attention items across all images in the three rounds. There was a significant correlation r(148) = .70 p < .001.
This indicates that there was a strong association between how much nature clicks there were in each of the attention items.

Lastly, I also examined unconditional multilevel models where the mean of each of the rounds was nested within the image. For the first attention item, the interclass correlation was 94.87%, indicating that the mean across the three rounds were consistent. This was similar for the voluntary attention. The interclass correlation for the voluntary attention item was 95%.
